A sand dune that forms in the surf zone due to the action of waves and currents.
A type of sand dune formed by the action of wind and water, found in coastal environments.
A term used to describe the rough and irregular surface of concrete when it is too wet and insufficiently consolidated.
A term used to describe the rapid growth of an initially small crack in a structure under cyclic loading conditions.
A phenomenon during construction where the structure settles unevenly due to the varying resistance of soil layers, causing it to twist and tilt.
A type of soil composed of large sand grains that tend to cling together due to their spherical shape and cohesionless nature.
A local term for large sand dunes formed by wind action in coastal areas.
A term for a turbulent sea condition in which a ship is likely to be thrown over by a wave and wrecked.
A material or rock that contains a significant amount of calcium carbonate, typically in the form of the mineral calcite.
A material that is composed primarily of calcium carbonate, often found in deposits such as limestone and chalk.
A material composed primarily of calcium carbonate, often formed from the accumulation of marine organisms such as corals and shells.
A sedimentary rock composed primarily of calcium carbonate, typically formed from the accumulation of marine organisms' remains.
A material that contains a significant amount of calcium carbonate, which may dissolve or be removed under certain chemical conditions, potentially altering its mechanical properties.
It describes sediment or rock predominantly composed of calcium carbonate minerals, such as calcite or aragonite.
A material composed primarily of calcium carbonate, often found in sedimentary rocks like limestone and chalk.
A term used to describe sediment or rock composed primarily of calcite or aragonite, minerals that are soluble in acid.
A factor used to modify design seismic forces by accounting for the inherent ductility and overstrength of structural components.
A response modification factor that reduces design forces in a seismic force-resisting system by accounting for the structure's ability to dissipate energy through inelastic deformation.
A response modification factor that adjusts the design forces for structural components to account for their inelastic deformation capacity beyond yield.

A response modification factor applied to reduce design forces for ductile structural systems by accounting for their inherent ability to dissipate energy through inelastic deformation during seismic events.
It is a factor applied to the design forces to account for the inherent overstrength and ductility provided by an element of the seismic force-resisting system.
A factor that modifies the fundamental period of a structure to account for damping effects, specifically the ratio of the effective damping period to the undamped natural period.
A modification factor applied to the design forces in a structure to account for its inherent overstrength and ductility, allowing for reduced seismic demands in the design process.
A response modification factor that modifies the seismic base shear force to account for the system's inelastic behavior under seismic loading.
Points with known or established horizontal and vertical positions used for comparison and adjustment during surveying and mapping projects.
Points whose coordinates are accurately determined and used as reference to adjust the coordinates of other survey points.
Reference points of known elevation used to ensure the accuracy of topographic survey measurements.
Geometric reference markers whose coordinates are precisely established and used to validate the accuracy of survey measurements.
Points whose coordinates are known and used to adjust measurements to ensure accuracy.
Fixed points with known coordinates used as reference for surveying and alignment checks.
Reference marks with known coordinates used to compare survey measurements and assess accuracy in geodetic surveys.
Points with known or established elevations used to adjust and calibrate surveying instruments or measurements.
The maximum stress intensity factor at which a flaw can exist without causing crack propagation in a material.
The maximum stress intensity factor at which a crack remains stable under loading, beyond which fracture initiates.
The maximum stress intensity factor at which a crack will not propagate under cyclic loading, representing the material's resistance to fatigue crack growth.
A material property representing the maximum stress intensity at which a crack can propagate under plane stress conditions, determining the threshold for crack initiation or stable growth.
The maximum stress intensity factor at which a crack will not extend under cyclic loading, used to determine the fatigue life of a structure under sustained stress.
A material property representing the maximum stress intensity at which a crack will not propagate under static loading, beyond which fracture occurs.
A material property representing the maximum stress intensity at which a crack will not propagate under plane strain conditions.
The maximum stress intensity factor at which a crack in a material will not propagate under cyclic loading.
A wall or structure made entirely of masonry units laid in mortar without embedded steel reinforcement.
A structural material composed of masonry units laid in mortar without reinforcing steel to resist seismic forces.
A structural material composed of masonry units laid in mortar without steel reinforcement to resist tensile stresses.
A structural material composed of masonry units laid in mortar without steel reinforcement to resist tensile stresses.
A construction material composed of masonry units laid in mortar without steel reinforcement to resist tensile stresses.
A structural material composed of masonry units laid in mortar without steel reinforcement to resist tensile and shear forces.
A structural material comprising masonry units laid in mortar without reinforcing steel to resist applied loads.
A construction material composed of masonry units bonded with mortar but lacking steel reinforcement to resist tensile stresses.
A structure that allows two intersecting roadways to cross over or under each other without their traffic mixing, typically constructed to eliminate at-grade intersections.
A structure that elevates or depresses one roadway relative to another to permit uninterrupted traffic flow at the intersection.
A structure that elevates or depresses one roadway relative to another to eliminate intersecting traffic flows and reduce congestion.
A structure that elevates or depresses one roadway relative to another to allow uninterrupted traffic flow between them.
A structure that elevates or depresses one roadway relative to another to allow uninterrupted traffic flow between them without intersection.
A structure that elevates or depresses one roadway relative to another to allow uninterrupted traffic flow without intersections.
A structure that elevates or depresses one roadway relative to another to prevent intersections and allow uninterrupted traffic flow between them.
A structure that elevates one roadway above another to allow uninterrupted traffic flow at road intersections without traffic signals or stop signs.
Structural walls constructed from wood or steel studs and sheathing that resist lateral forces by transferring shear between wood-sheathed elements through friction and mechanical interlock.
Structural panels constructed using wood or metal framing members and sheathing materials to resist lateral forces by transferring shear stresses through wood-shear connectors or embedded fasteners.
Structural components made of wood or metal studs that resist lateral forces by shear transfer through sheathing materials like oriented strand board or plywood.
Shear walls constructed from wood or cold-formed steel studs sheathing that resist lateral forces by transferring them through shear deformation in the sheathing.
Shear walls constructed using wood or steel light framing fasteners to resist lateral forces by transferring loads directly to foundation elements.
Constructed of wood studs and sheathing, these walls resist lateral forces through the shear transfer and nailing between the sheathing and framing.
A structural system where thinly sheathed wood panels or gypsum board resist lateral forces by developing shear transfer through their connection to framing members.
Structural elements composed of wood or steel studs and sheathing that resist lateral forces by transferring them through shear resistance and structural connections to the foundation.
The maximum amount of strain a structural component can sustain under load before experiencing a significant reduction in load-carrying capacity.
The ability of a structural member to sustain inelastic deformation beyond its yield point before losing its load-carrying capacity.
The maximum strain or displacement a structural component can sustain beyond yield without experiencing significant loss of load-carrying capacity or fracture.
The maximum strain or displacement a structural component can sustain beyond its elastic limit before significant strength loss occurs.
The amount of permanent deformation a structural component can sustain before its load-carrying capacity significantly diminishes due to an extreme seismic event.
The maximum strain a structural component can sustain beyond its elastic limit before significant loss of load-carrying capacity occurs.
The maximum strain a structural component can sustain before it reaches its fracture or failure limit under load.
The maximum inelastic strain a structural component can sustain before losing its load-carrying capacity.
Cements that achieve compressive strengths of 17.2 MPa (2500 psi) or more within eight hours after mixing and wetting to reduce initial set times and accelerate early strength development.
Cements that achieve high early strength within a short timeframe, typically less than 24 hours, enabling early formwork removal and faster construction progression.
Cements that develop high early strength gain in the first few hours after mixing.
Cements that develop strength rapidly, reaching high compressive strength in a short period of time, typically within a few hours or days.
Cements that achieve high early compressive strength within a few hours after mixing, enabling accelerated concrete setting and early form removal.
Cements that achieve early strength gains, with compressive strength developed rapidly within a few days, enabling accelerated construction schedules.
Cements that develop compressive strength at a faster rate than normal portland cements, particularly in the early stages of hydration.
Cements that achieve specified strength within three days of placement, allowing for earlier formwork removal and quicker construction progress.
A surface along which sliding failure is assumed to occur in the form of a circular arc through the soil mass.
A curved plane along which a soil mass tends to fail by rotation, resembling the arc of a circle.
A curved, concave surface along which sliding occurs in a soil mass, approximating the arc of a circle.
A surface along which a soil mass may potentially slide in a curved path resembling the arc of a circle.
A failure surface for soil slope stability analysis that approximates a curved path resembling the arc of a circle joining an upper and lower segment of a potential failure mass.
A surface along which a soil mass may fail by rotating about a point, forming an arc with a radius determined by the geometry of the slope and the soil properties.
A curved path along which sliding could potentially occur within a soil or rock mass, defined by the arc of a circle that passes through the centroid of a wedge-shaped failure block.
A surface along which a soil mass may potentially slide in a curved path resembling the arc of a circle.
The force intentionally introduced into a bolted joint during assembly to keep the joint tightly compressed under service loads.
A tensile force applied to a bolt to compress fitted parts and ensure tight clamping during service.
A tensile force intentionally introduced into a bolted joint to prevent relative movement between connected components under service loads.
The compressive stress intentionally introduced into a bolted connection by tightening the bolts to ensure contact under service loads.
A tensile force intentionally applied to the threads of a fastener during assembly to maintain contact between joined surfaces and ensure a secure connection.
A tensile force applied to a fastener during installation to maintain contact between joint surfaces under service loads and prevent relative motion.
The force applied to a bolt during its tightening process to achieve a desired level of stress in the connected components.
A tensile force intentionally applied to a fastener to maintain contact and prevent slippage between joined surfaces under load.

A methodology that determines design forces for structural components by calculating the internal stresses resulting from applied loads, then comparing these stresses to allowable limits to ensure structural integrity.
A method that determines the shear strength of a soil by gradually increasing applied stress until failure occurs, without requiring direct measurement of deformation.
A method for designing structural elements by ensuring they remain within specified stress limits under service loads to prevent cracking and maintain durability.

A method of designing reinforced concrete structures by directly satisfying the equilibrium and compatibility requirements of concrete and steel under applied loads to ensure structural safety and performance.
A method where the steel element is designed to resist applied loads by ensuring its stress remains below specified limits to prevent failure.
A method for proportioning reinforced concrete structural members by checking that the computed stresses under factored loads do not exceed the specified material strengths.
A method in which the allowable stresses in structural components are calculated and checked against specified limits to ensure compliance with design criteria.
A method of designating the maximum allowable stress for structural elements based on their material properties and service conditions, as specified in AISC and AWS guidelines.
A mechanical analogy representing a structure's deformation by replacing it with a beam supported by elastic springs to simulate soil-structure interaction.
A method that simplifies a foundation analysis by representing a structure as a beam supported by discrete or continuous springs to model soil interaction.

A structural analysis method that represents a concrete slab's behavior by idealizing it as a beam supported by discrete elastic springs to simulate the interaction between the slab and its underlying foundation.
A method that represents a structure's interaction with its foundation by approximating it as a beam supported by discrete spring elements to analyze shear transfer, settlement, and bearing capacity.
A method representing a foundation as a continuous beam supported by discrete springs to calculate soil-structure interaction forces.
A representation where a structural component is treated as a beam supported by elastic springs to simulate its interaction with underlying support systems.

In structural engineering, an equivalent beam-on-springs model represents a foundation system where the foundation is simulated as a beam supported by discrete springs that simulate soil resistance, allowing for analysis of deflections and interactions under applied loads.
A mathematical representation that replaces a continuous foundation with discrete springs to simulate the interaction between a structural member and its support.
A simplified structural model designed to represent key characteristics and behaviors of a specific building type and seismic hazard level for analytical evaluation.
A structural model representing a specific design scenario, used to evaluate seismic response characteristics and performance under standardized loading conditions.
A structural model developed to represent specific design characteristics for assessing seismic performance through analytical simulations.
A model representing a structural system designed to emulate the seismic response characteristics of a specific building type, used to develop or validate analysis methods or design guidelines.
A model representing the structural characteristics of a building prototype designed to evaluate seismic performance under specified loading conditions.
A representation of a structural system designed to explore the seismic response of a specific building type by systematically varying key parameters under controlled loading conditions.
A model representing the structural characteristics, materials, and design parameters of a specific building type to simulate its seismic response under varying ground motions.
A standardized model representing various structural characteristics used to evaluate seismic performance through analysis and testing.
A statistical technique that iteratively adds or removes variables from a regression model based on their significance to optimize the model's predictive power.
A technique that iteratively adds or removes variables from a regression model based on their statistical significance at each step.
A statistical method that systematically selects variables for inclusion in a model by assessing their significance at each step.
A statistical technique that sequentially adds or removes variables based on their significance to the model, aiming to identify the most influential factors affecting the dependent variable.
A method that systematically adds and removes variables from a regression model based on statistical criteria to identify the most significant predictors.
It is a method that iteratively adds or removes predictors from a regression model based on their statistical significance to determine the most influential variables.
A statistical technique that iteratively adds or removes variables from a regression model based on their significance to optimize model parsimony.
A statistical technique that incrementally adds or removes predictor variables from a regression model based on their significance at each step.
Structural forces acting perpendicular to the plane of a wall or diaphragm that can cause cracking, spalling, or failure of elements not designed to resist such loads.
Forces or accelerations that act perpendicular to the plane of a wall, causing it to bend or deform without twisting around its vertical axis.
Forces and deformations induced by ground motion that act perpendicular to the plane of a structural wall or diaphragm, potentially causing bending, cracking, and buckling.
Forces and deformations acting perpendicular to the plane of a structural wall or diaphragm, potentially causing failure modes such as buckling or shear failure.
Forces acting perpendicular to the plane of a wall that can cause cracking, flexural damage, or out-of-plane collapse under seismic loading.
Forces and moments applied to structural elements that act perpendicular to their plane, causing bending and potential instability under seismic loading.
Loading conditions where structural components, such as walls or slabs, experience lateral forces perpendicular to their plane, potentially leading to out-of-plane bending and cracking.
Forces and moments applied to structural walls that act perpendicular to their plane, potentially causing cracking and shear failure.
Values that define the stiffness, yield strength, and strength degradation of a structural component by representing its behavior as a two-segment line with distinct elastic and inelastic properties.
Parameters that define a curve with two linear segments, each described by a slope and a transition point, used to model the relationship between seismic input and structural response in analysis.

Quantitative values that define a two-line graph representing the relationship between stress and strain for a material, including the yield strength and yield strain at the point of transition from elastic to plastic behavior.
Quantitative values representing the yield strength, yield plateau, and post-yield hardening characteristics of a material's stress-strain relationship modeled as a bilinear curve.
Values representing the yield strength, ultimate strength, and strain at each point on a graph that connects two straight lines to approximate an actual stress-strain curve.
Parameters that define a two-segment linear relationship used to model the load-displacement behavior of structural components, including yield point, yield strength, and post-yield stiffness.

Quantitative metrics that describe the elastic and plastic behavior of a material by defining initial elastic stiffness, yield strength, yield deformation, and ultimate deformation in a two-segment graphical representation.
Quantities that describe the shape of a curve formed by connecting two line segments to model a material's stress-strain relationship under nonlinear loading conditions.
A structural arrangement where forces from seismic or gravitational loads are reliably transferred through interconnected elements to the foundation without interruption.

A structural arrangement that ensures all forces generated by seismic or other lateral loading are transferred directly and uninterruptedly from any point in the building to the foundation without abrupt changes in direction or capacity.
A structural system that allows forces to flow unimpeded from their point of origin to the ground, transferring them through interconnected elements without abrupt changes in direction or resistance.
A structural system where loads from any point can be transmitted uninterrupted to the foundation through interconnected elements, ensuring structural integrity.
A structural system designed to transfer seismic forces from their point of origin through the building's components to the foundation without interruption.
A structural arrangement ensuring that seismic forces are consistently directed from the point of application to the ultimate point of resistance through uninterrupted connections and members.

A structural arrangement that ensures unobstructed transfer of lateral forces from any point in a building to its seismic force-resisting system through interconnected members without discontinuities.
A structural system where loads are transmitted from their point of application to the foundation without interruption, ensuring that they are resisted and distributed throughout the structure.
A phenomenon where structural components repeatedly experience changes in stress or deformation due to cyclic loading, leading to potential damage accumulation and failure over time.
A failure mode where materials experience cumulative damage under repeated thermal cycles, leading to a gradual reduction in their structural integrity over time.
The condition where repetitive loading and unloading of a structure over a period of time causes it to accumulate damage that may eventually lead to failure or disruption.
A process in which a material undergoes repeated cyclic stress or strain, leading to cumulative damage and eventual failure under prolonged loading conditions.
A phenomenon where materials subjected to repeated loading cycles experience a gradual loss of strength and stiffness due to the accumulation of micro-damage over time.

A phenomenon in which repeated loading and unloading of a soil element under dynamic seismic forces progressively reduces its shear strength and stiffness over time due to accumulated damage from cyclic loading.
A phenomenon where repeated loading and unloading cycles cause progressive damage in a structural component, leading to reduced load-carrying capacity over time.
A progressive deterioration in material strength and stiffness that occurs under repeated loading cycles, potentially leading to structural failure.
A radial gate that rotates about a horizontal axis to control water flow by adjusting its angle relative to the current.
A curved, radial gate that rotates about a horizontal axis at the top to control water flow in a spillway.
A curved, radial gate that rotates about a horizontal axis to control water flow in spillways or culverts.
A radial gate that rotates about a horizontal axis to control water flow in a spillway or outlet.
A curved, radial gate operated by a rotating arm to control water flow in spillways or navigation locks.
A curved radial gate that rotates about a horizontal axis to control water flow in circular culverts or culverts with wicket piers.
A large curved gate that rotates about a horizontal axis to control water flow in a spillway.
A curved, radial gate that rotates vertically around a horizontal axis to control water flow in a spillway.
A geologic hazard caused by rapid liquefaction-induced lateral ground displacements in saturated fine-grained soils, leading to potential instability of slopes and structures.
A type of mass movement where saturated soil or sediment flows downslope parallel to the coast due to liquefaction triggered by seismic shaking or other rapid loading.
Shallow-seated, rapid downslope movements of unconsolidated, water-saturated sediments triggered by strong ground shaking.

Lateral spreads are ground movements resulting from liquefaction that cause the ground to spread laterally away from areas of higher elevation, often leading to significant structural damage or failure.
A phenomenon where weak, saturated sediments lose strength and flow laterally downslope during an earthquake due to liquefaction.
A type of soil deformation where large, horizontal movements occur along a slope due to liquefaction-induced loss of shear strength.
A geologic phenomenon where saturated, cohesionless soils liquefy and flow laterally downslope due to strong ground shaking.
A phenomenon where soil and structures slip and flow downslope due to lateral shaking during earthquakes.

A ground motion intensity derived by combining the maximum considered earthquake (MCE) ground motion with site-specific probabilistic and deterministic hazard values, tailored to achieve a specified risk level for seismic design.
Ground motion values derived by combining site-specific probabilistic and deterministic hazard analyses to define the maximum seismic demand a structure must withstand for specified risk levels.

A ground motion intensity derived from probabilistic and deterministic seismic hazard analyses to represent the maximum potential earthquake shaking that structural designs must withstand, tailored by site-specific response spectra analysis to account for potential liquefaction or lateral spreading effects.

A ground motion intensity derived by scaling the maximum considered earthquake ground motion to achieve a specified probability of exceedance over a specified period, tailored to the site's seismic hazard.

A seismic hazard level derived from probabilistic and deterministic analyses to define an upper-bound ground motion spectrum that accounts for the potential for exceedance of specified earthquake magnitudes and attenuation relationships at a site.
Site-specific seismic ground motions determined by combining the probabilistic and deterministic hazard analysis to meet specified probabilistic and intensity-based criteria defined by ASCE/SEI 7-22.

The seismic hazard level derived from probabilistic and deterministic ground motion analyses, adjusted by site-specific factors and scaled to incorporate upper-bound estimates, representing the maximum demand expected for design in a given location.

Ground motion parameters derived from probabilistic and deterministic seismic hazard analyses, scaled to a specified structural collapse probability, to ensure a building’s seismic design meets the target level of safety for the site.
Quantitative metrics that, when exceeded, indicate a project’s inability to meet performance objectives and trigger re-evaluation or remedial actions.
Absolute values that quantify specific safety margins for structural analysis, ensuring that response quantities like moment or shear remain within predetermined thresholds to prevent failure.
Quantitative indicators that define the boundaries within which a structural component must operate to achieve or maintain its desired performance level under design loading.
Conditions that, when exceeded during construction, indicate the necessity for corrective measures to maintain the structural integrity and performance of the project.
Quantitative values derived from fragility analysis that define thresholds for structural repair costs and repair time exceeding 10% of median replacement cost and median repair time, respectively.
Quantitative or narrative bounds established to evaluate whether a project's specific performance attribute meets the required outcome and ensure compliance with established criteria.
Quantitative measures established for structural, nonstructural, or operational components to identify their ability to withstand seismic forces and remain operable or functional after an earthquake.
Structural boundary conditions or dimensions that directly influence the seismic performance of a building component, such as height, aspect ratio, or aspect ratio of opening.
A model or system that represents the behavior of a larger or real-world structure under earthquake loading for testing and validation purposes.
A full-scale, physical model of a hydraulic structure or system used to study flow patterns, sediment transport, and other hydraulic behaviors under operating conditions.
A full-scale representation of a physical structure or system used to study and validate design principles in their actual operating environment.
A full-scale model of a structure or system used to study its behavior under realistic environmental conditions.
The actual construction, design, or structure that serves as a reference or standard for comparison.
A model that closely emulates the behavior of a physical structure or system under actual load conditions to validate its design and performance.
It is the physical test structure used to determine the required information about the foundation and its underlying strata.
A physical structure built to replicate the size, shape, and flow conditions of a real-world dam or spillway for experimental testing and validation of design assumptions.
Describes points on a survey network where both points can see each other directly without obstructions.
A condition where two points can see each other directly without obstruction.
Two points are said to be intervisible if a direct line of sight exists between them without any obstruction.
A condition where two points on a survey line can see each other directly without obstruction.
A situation where two points on the surface of the earth can see each other directly without obstruction.
Adjective describing a condition where two survey marks can be directly seen and measured from each other without obstruction.
A condition where two survey points can see each other directly without any obstruction in between.
A condition where two or more survey points can directly see each other without obstruction.
A structure that moves vertically within a guide wall to control water flow by raising or lowering to create or release a pool of water.
A structure that moves upward between guides to control water flow by fully opening or closing a channel without obstructing navigation.
A structure that raises or lowers perpendicular to the water surface to regulate flow or drain water from a channel without changing the water depth.
A structure where the gate moves upward in a vertical direction, controlled by a hoist mechanism, to regulate water flow and maintain desired water levels in a canal or spillway.
A structure that raises or lowers perpendicularly to control water flow in a navigation dam, operated by vertical movement of its leaf.
A structure that raises and lowers perpendicular to the flow of water by means of vertical lifting mechanisms.
A structure that moves straight upward and downward on vertical guides to control water flow in a spillway or navigation dam.
A structure that moves straight upward between guides to regulate water flow by opening or closing a channel.
A soil profile characterized by very high natural seismic response due to high liquefaction potential, very soft fine-grained saturated soils, or very deep soils with extremely high plasticity.
A soil profile characterized by very high liquefaction potential or very thick soft soils, requiring site-specific evaluation for seismic response.
A soil profile with very high liquefaction potential and very high nonlinear soil response that may result in extreme ground motion amplification.

A soil profile where the average shear wave velocity in the uppermost 30 meters (100 feet) is less than 60 m/s (200 ft/s), indicating very soft soil susceptible to significant liquefaction and high ground motion amplification.
A soil profile characterized by very high liquefaction potential and very deep soft soil, requiring the most stringent seismic design criteria.
A soil profile characterized by very high soil liquefaction potential and/or very soft to extremely soft soil conditions, requiring specific seismic design criteria.
A soil profile where the average shear wave velocity in the top 30 meters is less than 180 meters per second, characterized by very high liquefaction potential and extreme site response.
A soil profile characterized by very high liquefaction potential and peak ground motions exceeding 2.5 times those on hard rock.
Loads that repeatedly change in magnitude or direction over time due to dynamic forces such as ground shaking in an earthquake.
Repeated applications of stress or deformation to a structural component that vary in magnitude and direction over a defined number of cycles.
Alternating stresses applied to a structure during its service life that repeatedly reverse in direction.

A graphical representation that describes how a structural element's resistance (force) varies with its deformation under applied loads.
A graphical or analytical representation that relates the applied force to the resulting deformation in a structural component or system.
A graphical or analytical representation that describes the relationship between the applied force and the resulting deformation in a structural component or material.
A graphical or mathematical representation that describes how a structural component's resistance (force) changes as it deforms under applied loads.
A graphical or analytical representation that describes how much a structural component deflects under applied loads, defining its stiffness and ultimate capacity.
A graphical or analytical representation that illustrates how a structural component's resistance changes in response to increasing deformation under applied loads.
A curve that describes the behavior of a structural component by plotting applied force against its corresponding deformation at failure.
A parameter describing the relative length of the effective shear span of a structural member to its total depth, used to assess its susceptibility to shear failure.
The ratio of the shear span length to the effective depth of a structural component, used to classify its behavior under shear loading.
The ratio of the distance from the support to the point of load application to the effective depth of the beam, used to categorize shear-critical regions in reinforced concrete design.

The ratio of the distance from the support to the point of maximum moment in a structural member to the effective depth of that member, indicating the relative influence of shear forces in determining its behavior.
The dimensionless ratio of the effective shear span to the effective depth of a structural concrete member, used to classify its behavior under shear forces.
The ratio of the distance between the support points to the depth of the beam, used to classify structural elements as deep or shallow beams for design purposes.
The ratio of the effective shear span to the effective depth of a structural component, which influences its shear strength and failure mode.
The ratio of the effective shear span to the effective depth of a structural member, used to assess its vulnerability to shear failure.
The maximum angle a structural component can sustain beyond its yield point before it loses its load-carrying capacity due to significant inelastic deformation.
The maximum angular deformation a structural component can sustain beyond its yield point before undergoing significant loss of load-carrying capacity.

A measure quantifying a structural component's ability to undergo inelastic deformation beyond its yield point before reaching failure, expressed as the ratio of its ultimate rotation to the yield rotation.
The angle through which a structural element can rotate beyond its yield point before significant strength loss occurs.
The angle, measured in radians, beyond the yield point at which a structural component can deform without losing its load-carrying capacity.
The maximum angle a structural component can sustain beyond its elastic limit before significant loss of load-carrying capacity occurs due to inelastic deformation.
A measure of the total angle through which a structural component can deform beyond its elastic limit before significant degradation in strength or loss of stability occurs.

The maximum angle through which a reinforced concrete structural component can sustain beyond its elastic limit before significant deterioration occurs, indicating its ductility and capacity to resist deformation under seismic loading.
A coefficient that adjusts the applied live load to account for how the load is shared among multiple girder lines within a bridge cross-section during design and analysis.
A numerical coefficient applied to the live load to account for the reduction in the maximum design force due to the spread of vehicle weight across multiple girders in a bridge cross-section.

A numerical coefficient applied to live load effects to account for the reduction in load effects on individual structural components due to the redistribution of loads across multiple supports or spans.

A factor applied to live load effects to account for the portion of the applied load that is transmitted to a specific structural component due to the distribution of load across multiple supports or segments.
A dimensionless factor that represents the ratio of the total applied live load to the portion of that load distributed to a specific structural element in a bridge cross-section.
A dimensionless factor applied to the live load to account for the portion of the load that is actually carried by a specific structural component within a bridge section.
A coefficient applied to live load effects to account for the influence of adjacent traffic in determining the design forces for structural components.
A numerical factor applied to the live load effect to account for the spatial variation in distribution of vehicular loads across multiple girders in a bridge cross-section.
A ratio quantifying the structural deformation remaining after earthquake demands are applied, expressed as the relative displacement between top and bottom of a building divided by its height.
The ratio of the additional story drift caused by residual displacement after a seismic event to the expected yield story drift at the onset of significant inelastic deformation.
The ratio of the residual story drift to the building height that persists after the removal of the applied loading to simulate the loss of the last strength mechanism in the analysis.
The ratio of the story drift after the seismic-forced displacement is subtracted from the total drift.
A parameter that quantifies the expected lateral deformation of a structure beyond its initial yield point, used to assess the potential for collapse under seismic loading.
The ratio of the additional seismic deformation that remains after initial yielding has occurred, representing the post-yield deformation component.
The remaining lateral displacement of a structural component relative to its initial position after the applied load is removed.
The ratio of the residual deformation of a structural component to its original height, representing the permanent deformation that remains after the structure is released from a seismic load.
Low-lying regions inundated by floodwaters during high river stages and subject to periodic inundation from adjacent streams.
Low-lying areas adjacent to rivers or streams that inundate during high-water periods due to the elevation of water levels upstream.
Low-lying regions prone to flooding during high-water events due to their inability to drain efficiently.
Low-lying regions adjacent to rivers where water levels can rise during flood events, potentially inundating the area and causing damage to infrastructure.
Regions where surface water accumulates and remains stagnant due to inundation by high river levels, creating wetland environments characterized by slow-moving or standing water.
Regions of wetlands adjacent to river channels where water levels are influenced by the upstream influences and are inundated during high river stages.
Regions where the water level is elevated by a dam, creating shallow, marshy habitats that support diverse aquatic vegetation and wildlife.
Regions along river channels where floodwaters temporarily inundate forested wetlands due to high river stages.
The portion of a bridge that carries the roadway and its traffic above the supporting substructure and abutments.
The portion of a bridge that spans the opening and supports the deck, comprising girders or trusses that transfer loads to the substructure.
The structural components that span the gap between supports and carry the deck and traffic loads for a bridge.
The primary load-carrying portion of a bridge that spans the gap between supports and carries the traffic load.
The structural component of a bridge that spans between supports and carries the bridge deck and applied loads.
The component of a bridge that spans between supports and carries traffic loads, often consisting of girders and decking.
The portion of a bridge above the deck that supports the roadway and spans over the bridge substructure.
The portion of a bridge that carries the roadway and supports above the abutments or piers.
Collaborative arrangements where federal agencies work with state and local entities to share resources and expertise in implementing environmental and infrastructure projects.
A collaborative arrangement among federal, state, and local agencies to collectively fund, manage, and implement infrastructure projects, leveraging their respective resources and jurisdictions.
A collaborative arrangement where federal agencies, state departments, and local governments work together to share resources, expertise, and funding for public infrastructure projects.
Collaborative arrangements between federal agencies, state governments, and local authorities aimed at leveraging resources and expertise to implement large-scale infrastructure projects.
Collaborative agreements between federal, state, and local entities to establish and maintain flood risk management programs.

Collaborative arrangements where the federal government, state agencies, and local authorities work together to fund, develop, and manage infrastructure projects, leveraging each level's strengths and resources.

An arrangement where federal agencies, state governments, and local authorities collaborate to share resources, expertise, and responsibilities for implementing flood risk reduction projects, leveraging their respective strengths and authorities to achieve comprehensive and effective flood management solutions.
Collaborative efforts among federal, state, and local governments to share resources, expertise, and funding for transportation infrastructure projects.
A weld produced by rotating one member while continuously adding filler metal to create a joint between two surfaces with a uniform circumferential overlap.
A repair weld made in a damaged region of a steel member to restore its structural integrity by filling the defect with molten steel.
A weld formed by depositing weld metal in a single pass without utilizing a backing material.
A weld joining two plates at right angles to form an angled corner, requiring precise positioning of the plates to ensure proper alignment.
A welding process where the heat required for fusion is supplied solely by the resistance to the passage of an electric current through the joint.
A weld made using resistance spot welding, in which two or more metal parts are joined by the heat generated at the interface under pressure from the application of electric current.
A fusion weld produced by heating the workpieces to the plastic state and applying pressure to form a solid bond without additional filler metal.
A weld in which the weld face is prepared by cutting a groove to a specific depth and angle, and the weld metal is deposited in that groove to join two portions of a material.
A device that measures concrete strength by comparing the rebound of a spring-driven hammer against the surface, calibrated for use underwater.
A device that measures the rebound of a steel mass against concrete to estimate its compressive strength, with the hammer reshaped to resist water ingress and moisture effects.

A device that measures the surface hardness of concrete by recording the rebound of a spring-loaded mass against the surface, with the aim of estimating compressive strength through empirical correlations.

A device that measures the surface hardness of concrete by projecting a small dart at a known velocity and determining the rebound distance, which correlates to compressive strength without requiring water immersion.
A device that measures the surface hardness of concrete by measuring the rebound height of a spring-loaded mass, an indicator of compressive strength, by firing a spring-loaded mass at the surface.

A device that measures the surface hardness of concrete by recording the rebound distance of a spring-driven hammer and compensating for variations in moisture content by incorporating waterproofing technology.

A device that measures the hardness of concrete by launching a spring-loaded mass against its surface and interpreting the rebound distance as an indicator of compressive strength, while also accounting for the influence of moisture.

An instrument that measures concrete's surface hardness by launching a spring-driven mass and calculating rebound distance, adjusted for moisture and surface conditions, to estimate compressive strength indirectly.
A condition where the nut fails to tighten or loosen smoothly due to thread damage or deformation, often caused by over-tightening, cross-threading, or foreign debris.
A method for tightening a nut by applying torque to the nut itself while keeping the bolt stationary, often used in situations where direct access to the bolt head is limited.
The measurement of the distance a threaded fastener needs to be tightened by rotating its nut a specified number of turns.
A fastener that is tightened by rotating the nut relative to the bolt, which remains stationary during assembly.
A method for locking a bolt in place by tightening it incrementally to ensure secure fastening.
The angle through which a threaded fastener's nut must be rotated to tighten or loosen it by a specific amount, determined by the fastener's pitch and lead.
The coefficient representing the ratio of the nut's rotational displacement to the linear displacement of the screw thread in a threaded assembly.
A method that tightens a pipe joint by cranking a wrench to rotate a nut against the threads of a pipe, requiring at least two workers and often using a pipe wrench and a socket wrench.
The point on the surface of the water at which the water surface intersects a vertical plane normal to the major axis of the reservoir.
The longitude at which the normal phase of the tide occurs at a specific location relative to a reference time.
The angular location of the north end of a baseline on a reference ellipsoid.
A reference point on a ship's hull that indicates the last longitudinal bulkhead position, used to describe the ship's structure and storage capacity.
The nominal longitude of a point, representing the longitude assigned to a location for reference purposes.
The component of a vector that represents the longitudinal component of the weight of the vessel acting on the keel.
The greatest longitude at which the tidal range exceeds 1.5 m due to diurnal inequality.
The angular coordinate that measures an object's position east or west of the prime meridian.
The resistance of a structural wall to deformation in the plane perpendicular to its axis, quantified as the force per unit lateral displacement.
A measure of a structural wall's resistance to lateral forces per unit displacement, determined by its material properties, geometry, and boundary conditions.
The resistance of a structural wall to deformation in the direction perpendicular to its length, affecting its ability to distribute seismic forces to the foundation.
The resistance provided by the wall to prevent lateral displacement under seismic loads, calculated as the ratio of lateral force to lateral displacement.
The resistance of a structural wall to deformation under lateral loads, quantified as the slope of the load-deformation curve, typically expressed in kN/mm or lb/in.
The property of a structural wall that describes its ability to resist lateral (horizontal) forces applied in its plane by providing resistance through bending and shear deformation.
The resistance provided by a structural wall to lateral loads, quantified as the ratio of lateral load to lateral displacement at a specific point.
The resistance of a structural wall to horizontal deformation under applied loads, quantified by its stiffness in the direction perpendicular to its longitudinal axis.
The process by which adsorbed ions, gases, or molecules are released from the surface of a material upon removal of the adsorbing medium.
The process by which organic contaminants are released from surface sediments into the overlying water column due to changes in environmental conditions.
The process by which water or another fluid is released from a soil sample as the surrounding pressure is reduced.
The process by which water is removed from the soil by evaporation, vegetation, and other surface processes without being returned to the water table.
It is the process where a substance or component is released and removed from a material's surface or interior due to an applied force or change in environmental conditions.
The process by which water and solutes are released from soil particles and return to the groundwater reserve upon drying and rewetting cycles.

The process by which adsorbed molecules or ions, previously bound to a surface, are released back into the surrounding medium under favorable conditions such as changes in pH, temperature, or chemical environment.

The process in which previously adsorbed or absorbed molecules leave the surface or material to which they were attached due to changes in temperature or pressure, thereby reducing the concentration of the adsorbed phase.
A method of connecting sheet piling by overlapping adjacent sections vertically and securing them with bolts or welds to maintain alignment and prevent lateral movement.
A means of maintaining water levels between adjacent canals by allowing water to flow freely between them without obstructing navigation.
Interlocks that allow trains to move freely in both directions through adjacent tracks without the need for fixed barriers or signals.
A method that distributes the contact between two tires by dividing the tire surface into smaller areas to reduce wear.
A method of interlocking concrete masonry units where individual stones are interlocked across adjacent courses to prevent horizontal movement and maintain stability in retaining walls.
Mechanisms that maintain the structural integrity of interlocking concrete pavement by allowing air and moisture to escape between adjacent blocks.
Mechanical couplings that allow for axial alignment adjustments by sliding one component into another through openings designed to overlap.
Holding devices that secure track with two or more vertically spaced wedges to interlock the top of the sleepers and prevent longitudinal movement.
The ratio of the seismic displacement at which a structural system loses its load-carrying capacity to its elastic displacement under design-level ground motions.

A measure that quantifies the ability of a structural system to deform beyond its elastic limit through cyclic loading, determined by the ratio of the ultimate displacement at failure to the yield displacement.
The ratio of ultimate displacement to yield displacement for a structural system, representing its ability to undergo significant inelastic deformation before failure.
A measure of a structure’s ability to sustain large deformations beyond its yield point under seismic loading without losing its load-carrying capacity.

The ratio of the maximum displacement a structural component can sustain under cyclic loading to the displacement at its yield point, reflecting its ability to undergo significant deformation beyond initial yielding.
A measure of a structural system's ability to dissipate energy through inelastic deformation under seismic loading, quantified by the ratio of the displacement at collapse to the yield displacement.

A measure of a structural component's ability to sustain large inelastic deformations without sudden loss of load-carrying capacity, quantified by the ratio of its ultimate deformation to its yielding deformation.
A measure of a structural system's ability to sustain large deformations beyond its elastic limit through inelastic mechanisms such as yield and redistribution of forces within its components.
The cross-sectional area of a vessel's hull at its widest point, used to calculate its buoyancy and stability.
The area enclosed within the midship section of a vessel, determined by the horizontal projection of its shape at the mid-length point along its waterline.
The area of the hull cross-section at the center of the vessel's length, calculated as the product of the beam and draught.
The area of the cross-section at the center of a ship's length, calculated by averaging the areas of the sections at the forward and aft perpendiculars.
The cross-sectional area of a ship at its centerline, unaffected by any camber or deadrise, used to calculate the submerged volume for stability assessments.
The area of the cross-section of a ship at its widest point, determined by measuring the breadth at the center of the hull.
The area of the cross-section of a ship at its centerline, measured perpendicular to the length of the hull.
The area of the cross-section of a ship at its midpoint between the stern and bow.
The maximum rotational deformation a structural component can undergo beyond its yield point before it reaches complete plastic deformation, defining its ductility limit under loading.
A deformation metric representing the maximum rotational capacity a structural component can sustain before it fails due to excessive deformation.
The maximum deformation a structural component can sustain beyond its yield point before significant strength loss occurs.
The maximum rotation a structural component can undergo before it loses its ability to sustain further deformation due to plastic hinging.
The angle at which the structure undergoes significant degradation in strength and energy dissipation capacity due to excessive plastic deformation in its critical components.
The maximum rotational deformation a structural component can sustain beyond its yield point before significant loss in load-carrying capacity occurs.
The maximum rotation a structural component can sustain before its load-carrying capacity deteriorates due to plastic deformation.
The maximum angle a beam can sustain beyond which it loses its ability to resist further deformation due to yielding of reinforcing steel.
Quantifiable objectives established to evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of an organization's operations in achieving targeted outcomes.
Objectives that specify the desired level of water quality improvement or pollutant load reduction a treatment system must achieve during operation.
A statement that describes the desired outcomes or achievements a project aims to accomplish during or after completion to ensure it meets its intended purpose and objectives.
A set of desired outcomes for a project, established to guide the design process and ensure that the final construction meets specified requirements for functionality, durability, and safety.
Quantitative measures that specify desired levels of system efficiency, reliability, and safety to be achieved through engineering design.
Quantitative targets set by a project team to guide the development of a new building design, which are then used to evaluate and compare alternative design approaches.
Quantifiable objectives that guide the development of test procedures to ensure that structural components meet specified design criteria and safety standards.

Quantitative measures that explicitly define the desired outcomes and operational targets of a project or system, ensuring that performance is effectively managed and evaluated against predefined standards and objectives.
The maximum height of concrete placement without reconsolidation or vibration to ensure uniform consolidation and density.

The maximum vertical distance between the top surface of a previously placed concrete layer and the bottom surface of the next layer, within which concrete can be placed without additional consolidation.
The maximum height to which concrete can be placed in a single operation without reconsolidation.
The maximum height to which concrete should be placed in a single continuous layer during placement to ensure proper consolidation and prevent segregation.
The maximum thickness of concrete placed in a single pour to prevent excessive temperature rise and maintain uniformity within a structural element.
The maximum height of compacted soil placed in a single layer during construction, determined by equipment capabilities and material properties to ensure adequate compaction.
The maximum height to which concrete material can be placed in a single layer before compaction to produce a cohesive and dense mass.
The thickness of concrete placed in a single pour that is less than the maximum allowable lift height to ensure proper consolidation and structural integrity.
The largest bending moment that a structural component experiences during its service life, considering the effects of applied loads and system behavior.
The maximum bending moment that a structural component can sustain before it reaches its yielding strength.
The maximum moment that occurs at the critical section of a beam where plastic hinges are assumed to form under design loading conditions.
The maximum flexural moment experienced at a point in a structural component during its design loading condition, determined by analyzing the member's geometric and loading characteristics.
The maximum bending moment a structural component can sustain before it enters the plastic range of its stress-strain relationship.
The maximum moment experienced by a structural member before it yields at its critical section during the loading process.
The maximum bending moment at the center of the span for a simply supported beam when subjected to a uniformly distributed load.
The maximum bending moment experienced by a structural component during its loading history.
A method that determines structural demands by analyzing a set of earthquake ground motion components scaled to match specified response spectral values at predefined periods.

A method that derives forces and accelerations for a structural model by transforming acceleration-time data into equivalent static loads based on the structure's assumed natural frequencies and damping ratios.

A method that determines structural response by transforming seismic ground motion into a series of discrete spectral accelerations to assess the maximum dynamic forces acting on a structure at various vibration periods.
A method that determines the maximum response of a structure's fundamental mode of vibration to earthquake ground motion by plotting acceleration versus natural period.
A method to determine seismic forces by translating a ground motion's acceleration time history into a series of response accelerations at specific periods and damping ratios.
A method that determines structural demands by applying dynamic loads derived from earthquake ground motion to a modal analysis model to calculate maximum responses at each degree of freedom.
A method that determines structural demands by converting the ground motion's acceleration history into a set of spectral response accelerations at various periods to evaluate seismic forces.
A method that represents the maximum ground motion at each natural frequency as a series of pseudospectral accelerations to assess structural response.
A pipeline component designed to resist deformation under internal pressure by relying on its own structural stiffness rather than relying on external restraints or supporting materials.
A pipe that resists deformation under load due to its high stiffness, allowing it to transfer loads directly to supporting structures without significant flexing or bending.
A culvert with a concrete or steel lining that restricts deformation and maintains its shape under load.
A pipe that maintains contact between its ends and the surrounding soil under load, resisting internal pressure changes by relying on soil confining stress rather than inherent pipe stiffness.
A pipe that deforms elastically under load, with its behavior influenced by the stiffness of both the pipe material and the surrounding soil.
A pipe that does not deflect under load due to its high stiffness and ability to maintain its shape.
A pipe that resists deformation due to its stiff material properties and structural design, ensuring reliable performance under external loads.
A pipe that is designed to resist deformation and maintain its shape under load by transferring loads directly to surrounding soil.
A calculated downward movement of land derived from GPS measurements that accounts for the combined effects of vertical crustal motion and relative sea-level changes.
The lowering of land relative to a reference datum computed through numerical modeling of fluid withdrawal and compaction processes.
A process in which the gradual sinking of land relative to a reference datum is quantified using mathematical models that simulate the deformation of the Earth's crust under loading conditions.
A decrease in land elevation relative to a reference datum caused by the compaction of sedimentary basins due to fluid withdrawal.
A process where soil compaction or fluid extraction causes a gradual lowering of the land surface relative to a reference datum.
Downward movement of the ground surface resulting from the removal of fluids, often oil or gas, from underground reservoirs, calculated using mathematical models and historical compaction data.

A phenomenon where localized ground surface lowering occurs due to the compaction and consolidation of sediments in response to fluid withdrawal or structural loading, often measured through repeated leveling surveys or interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) analysis.

A reduction in land elevation caused by fluid withdrawal that results from mechanical compaction and is calculated through mathematical modeling based on measured reservoir changes and geotechnical parameters.
A layer of concrete applied by spraying to bond with and reinforce an existing concrete surface.
A layer of concrete applied to a structural surface by pneumatic means to restore or protect its integrity and performance.
A layer of concrete applied using pneumatic delivery to repair or protect existing concrete surfaces.
A layer of concrete sprayed onto a substrate to protect it from abrasion, erosion, or spalling by forming a strong, durable surface.
A layer of concrete applied by pneumatically projected means to a substrate to repair or protect structural components.
A layer of concrete applied to an existing structure using pneumatic pressure to form a protective or repair surface.
A layer of concrete sprayed onto a substrate to restore or enhance its structural integrity, durability, or appearance.
A layer of mortar or concrete applied by pneumatic projection to consolidate and protect existing concrete surfaces.
A phenomenon where the ground surface sinks at different rates and locations over time, altering its elevation in response to natural or human-induced processes.
A phenomenon where land elevation changes over time and across space due to natural and human-induced processes.
A process in which the elevation of a region changes over time and across space due to subsurface deformation induced by the withdrawal of fluids.

A phenomenon where the elevation of the Earth's surface gradually decreases over time and varies geographically due to natural or human-induced processes such as sediment compaction, aquifer depletion, or tectonic activity.
A phenomenon where the Earth's surface sinks at different rates and locations over time, influenced by natural processes such as tectonic activity, fluid withdrawal, and sediment compaction.
A phenomenon where the vertical displacement of Earth's surface relative to a reference datum changes both in space and time due to natural or human-induced processes.
A phenomenon where the elevation of a coastal area undergoes continuous downward displacement over time due to natural or human-induced mechanisms.
A phenomenon where the elevation of a site changes unpredictably over time due to localized geologic processes, including tectonic and natural compaction-related movements.
Buildings designed to remain operational following a damaging earthquake.

Infrastructure components essential for emergency response, such as hospitals, fire stations, and communication centers, designed to sustain structural integrity during earthquakes to ensure functionality.
Buildings, systems, or components whose destruction or disruption would have a significant impact on the national security, economy, or public health and safety of the United States.
Structures that require uninterrupted operation for public safety, national security, or economic stability, such as hospitals, water treatment plants, and emergency response centers.
Buildings or structures whose failure or loss of functionality could have severe impacts on safety, public health, or an economy.
Structures essential to the functioning of society that require protective measures during construction to maintain their operational integrity and safety.
Structures vital to the community's operation, requiring seismic design to ensure functionality and safety in the event of an earthquake.
Buildings that require continuous operation to support public safety and national security functions.
A parameter that adjusts the peak ground acceleration in a response spectrum to match the ground motion characteristics of a specific site, derived from the site-specific median response spectrum.
A numerical factor applied to the lateral force at each story level to account for overstrength and ductility in seismic-force-resisting systems assumed by ASCE/SEI 7-16.
A numerical factor applied to the design live load to account for the dynamic effects of live load repetition and impact on the structural response.
A factor applied to the peak ground acceleration to account for the site's soil type and amplifies the demand on structural components.
A factor used to adjust a load combination to account for the probability of multiple simultaneous loading events occurring.
A factor applied to the peak ground acceleration to account for soil amplification effects on structural response.
A factor applied to the peak moment in a beam to calculate equivalent distributed loads for design purposes.
A parameter that adjusts the probability of detecting slip events based on the magnitude of the slip motion, applied to slip-weakening friction laws to link slip rate to friction.
Data values that indicate the true value exceeds a specified threshold without providing the exact magnitude.
Observations where the true value lies beyond a measurable threshold but is not known precisely due to measurement limits.
Data where the value of a measurement is known to be above or below a certain threshold but the exact value is not available.
Data that are not fully observed because the true value was not measured but is known to exceed or fall below a certain threshold.
Data that is known to exceed a certain threshold but whose exact value remains unknown.
Data where some observations are partially observed due to truncation or left-hand censoring in the sampling process.
Data where the exact value of a variable is not observed but is known to be greater than or less than certain threshold values.
Data for which only the lower or upper bound of a parameter (e.g., yield strength) is known, not its exact value.
The maximum force or moment that a structural component is designed to resist without exceeding its material strength.
A standardized load used to calculate the design strength of structural members by applying it in various combinations to simulate expected service conditions.
The primary external force or combination of forces that directly induces the maximum design stresses and governs the structural component's design and sizing.
The primary or dominant force or force component that governs the design and behavior of a structural element or system.
A load that produces the largest tension or compression force in a member.
The load that governs the design of a structural component when compared to other loads based on their effect on stress or demand.
The force or combination of forces that determines the design and capacity of a structural component or system.
The maximum force or moment that a structural component experiences during its service life, used to design the component for strength and stability.
A structural component composed of an open-grid steel sheet with no concrete cover, designed to resist in-plane seismic forces by acting as a diaphragm within a structural system.

A structural component where a reinforced concrete slab is cast directly on top of a corrugated steel deck, acting as a composite diaphragm to transfer lateral forces in a building's seismic-force-resisting system without relying on shear studs.
A structural component in which steel deck panels directly transfer seismic forces between structural elements without additional concrete or other materials.

A structural component where steel decking forms the primary shear-resisting element without concrete fill, relying solely on its steel section to transfer lateral forces across a building's seismic-force-resisting system.
A structural component consisting of a steel deck without concrete fill that acts as a horizontal diaphragm to transfer lateral forces between supporting elements.
A structural component that relies solely on its steel surface to transfer seismic forces through shear and flexural actions without additional concrete topping.
A structural system where steel deck panels are welded directly to supporting members to form a continuous load-resisting horizontal diaphragm without concrete cover.

A structural system where steel deck panels with no applied concrete acting compositely with concrete fill serve as the primary horizontal load-resisting element by developing shear resistance through mechanical interlock.
A method of reinforcing concrete columns by encasing them in additional concrete to improve their load-carrying capacity and ductility.
A process in which a concrete or masonry column is encased with steel plates or other materials to increase its compressive and flexural strength and improve its seismic performance.
Enclosing a structural column with concrete or steel to improve its resistance to seismic forces and deformation.
A method of reinforcing existing concrete columns by wrapping them with a high-strength steel or fiber-reinforced polymer sheath.
A technique that encases concrete columns with steel plates to improve their seismic performance.
A process of adding external concrete or steel shells to existing concrete columns to increase their load-carrying capacity and improve their ductility and seismic performance.
A construction method in which a new concrete layer is applied over the exposed surface of an existing concrete structure to repair or strengthen it.
A method of strengthening existing concrete columns by encasing them with additional concrete or fiber-reinforced polymer sheets to improve their load-carrying capacity and ductility.
A zone in a structural member where the curvature reverses due to the application of loads, resulting in compressive stresses on the top fibers and tensile stresses on the bottom fibers.
A portion of a concrete deck slab where the steel reinforcement is exposed to tensile stress due to the curvature of the structural member.
A structural zone within a concrete beam where the applied loads cause the bottom fibers to be in compression while the top fibers are in tension.

A segment of a structural member where the applied loads induce curvature in the opposite direction to that of positive bending, resulting in compressive stresses on the top surface and tensile stresses on the bottom surface.
A structural area where the curvature of the concrete flexural member is convex upwards, causing the bottom reinforcement to resist tensile stresses.
A section of a structural component where the moment results in compression on the top fiber and tension on the bottom fiber.

A section of a structural member where the moment causes the top fibers to be in compression and the bottom fibers to be in tension, often requiring additional reinforcement to resist cracking and cracking reinforcement.
A portion of a concrete deck slab where the steel reinforcement is subjected to tensile stress due to curvature in the opposite direction to that of the applied loads.
A component that is manufactured off-site and assembled on-site to provide a pathway for smoke and combustion gases to exit a wood stove or fireplace.
A component installed in a factory and shipped to the installation site as a complete unit, designed to vent combustion products from fireplaces or appliances directly to the outside.
A component manufactured in a controlled environment to provide a safe and efficient pathway for exhaust gases from a fireplace to the outdoors.
A chimney constructed off-site in a controlled environment and then transported and installed at the building site as a single unit.
A component assembled off-site and delivered as a complete unit for installation in a residential furnace or fireplace to safely vent combustion gases.
A structure manufactured off-site and installed to enclose and vent combustion gases from a wood-burning appliance directly into the exterior atmosphere.

A structural component manufactured off-site and designed to transport flue gases from a wood-burning appliance to the outdoors, meeting specific requirements for installation and performance without requiring mortar joints.
A chimney constructed entirely at a manufacturing facility and then transported to the installation site for assembly and connection to the fireplace.
The distance between the base of the structure and the bottom of the foundation that transmits structural loads directly into the underlying soil or rock.
The depth at which the concrete anchor is embedded into the foundation to provide resistance against uplift or overturning forces.
The depth to which a pile is driven into the soil to achieve sufficient embedment for transfer of structural loads into the foundation.
The distance below the bottom of the channel at which the scour depth stabilizes due to the presence of a structure.
The vertical dimension from the bottom of the footing to the deepest point of the soil mass into which the footing embeds, where the soil resists uplift forces and provides stability.
The vertical dimension required for a structural member to develop its design capacity by transferring load into a foundation material.
The depth to which a concrete-filled steel pile is embedded into the foundation material to resist uplift and overturning forces.
The vertical distance from the top of a pile to its embedded point within the supporting soil or concrete foundation, determining its resistance against vertical and horizontal loads.
Experimental measurements obtained during cyclic loading of a structural component to evaluate its nonlinear behavior and strength degradation under seismic excitation.
Information collected from in-service equipment to evaluate its performance and response under operating conditions, which can include vibration, displacement, and stress data.
Data obtained from experimental measurements or numerical simulations that represent the structural response to time-varying loads, used to verify and calibrate analytical models.
Information collected from experimental measurements of structural response to ground motion, used to assess seismic performance under actual loading conditions.
Information obtained from measurements of structural responses to applied loads or environmental motions that quantifies the behavior of a structure under dynamic conditions.
Information obtained from experimental measurements of a structure's response to seismic loading, used to validate and refine analytical models.
Measurements of structural response to seismic excitation obtained from accelerometers or other sensors installed on a building during an earthquake.
Information obtained from in situ measurements of a foundation's response to applied loads, revealing its stiffness and damping properties under operational conditions.
Devices installed at the ends of crane runways to limit the movement of cranes and prevent them from overrunning.
Devices installed at the ends of runway beams to limit the horizontal movement of a crane girder when it reaches the end of the runway.
Structural elements designed to restrain and control the movement of cranes within a building to prevent impacts with columns and other structural components.
Devices installed at the ends of runway beams or girders to limit the travel of a crane's trolleys or trucks and prevent overhang beyond the structural support.
Devices that limit the travel of a crane's trolley or bridge to prevent overhanging or excessive movement beyond designated work areas.
Devices installed at the end of runway beams to limit the horizontal movement of cranes beyond a certain point.
Devices installed at the ends of a runway to prevent cranes from overhanging the runway's end.
Devices installed at specified locations along a runway to limit the travel of cranes and prevent overhang beyond the runway edge.
