A device that detects and indicates the location of steel reinforcing bars within concrete structures.
A device that uses electromagnetic or acoustic waves to determine the depth and position of reinforcing steel bars within concrete structures.
A device that uses electromagnetic, ultrasonic, or ultrasonic pulse methods to detect and map the location and depth of reinforcing steel bars within concrete structures.
A device that uses electromagnetic or ultrasonic technology to detect the location and orientation of reinforcing steel within concrete structures.
A tool that detects the precise location and depth of reinforcing bars within concrete structures by generating and interpreting electromagnetic signals.
A device that detects the position of reinforcing steel bars within concrete structures using electromagnetic induction.
A fastening system that secures nonstructural elements to resist inertial forces and prevent damage or collapse during seismic events.
Measures designed to secure nonstructural items within a structure to prevent them from becoming projectiles during seismic shaking.
A system or device that secures nonstructural components to prevent them from becoming projectiles or falling during an earthquake.
Fasteners or attachments designed to secure nonstructural components to structural elements to resist seismic forces and prevent damage or detachment.
A device or method used to secure and fasten nonstructural components to their supports or an underlying structural element to resist seismic forces.
The fastening of secondary elements to structural walls to prevent collapse or excessive displacement during seismic events.
A device or system that restrains or supports a nonstructural component to prevent it from falling or being damaged during seismic motion.
A system designed to secure nonstructural elements to their supports or to each other in order to resist seismic forces and prevent damage or collapse during an earthquake.
A structural component that extends horizontally along the perimeter of a roof or floor deck, providing support and distribution of loads to the supporting foundation or wall.
A structural component installed around the outer perimeter of a concrete slab to provide lateral support and distribute loads to the foundation.

A structural member attached to the outer edge of the slab-on-ground to support the perimeter formwork and reinforce the concrete edge against lifting or displacement.
A horizontal structural member that connects the top of a basement wall to the floor framing above, transferring loads into the foundation and supporting the floor system.
A structural member encircling the perimeter of a roof deck to support and distribute concentrated loads from bearing walls.
A structural member located along the perimeter of a concrete slab that supports the slab edge and transfers loads to the foundation or supporting elements.
The square root of the average of the squared amplitudes of a signal's samples over a specified time interval, representing its effective magnitude.

A measure derived from the root mean square of a signal's amplitude to quantify its average power over time.
A metric representing the root mean square of the power received from a satellite's RF signal, used to indicate its relative intensity.

A non-destructive testing method that uses a dye to reveal discontinuities on the surface of a material.

A non-destructive testing method that uses a visible or fluorescent dye to detect surface-breaking defects in a material.
A random change in the initial tension introduced into a bolt during assembly, which can affect the stability and performance of bolted connections.
The change in tension between the high and low values of bolt tension introduced during installation, calculated as the difference between the maximum and minimum applied loads.

The range or deviation in the applied tension during fastener installation, which affects the reliability and performance of the connection.
The difference between the maximum and minimum values of tension in a bolt, resulting from manufacturing and installation tolerances.
The difference in tension between the highest and lowest bolts in a group, introduced by manufacturing and installation processes, which affects structural performance.

A graph that shows the probability of exceedance for multiple flood magnitudes, derived from a site's flood history or risk models.
A graphical representation showing the standardized relationship between water depth and frequency of exceedance for a location, derived from historical flood data.
A graphical representation that shows the probability of a flood event exceeding a specified water depth at a given location over time.
A graphical representation of the probability of exceeding a given ground motion intensity at a specific site, derived from seismic hazard analysis.
A graphical representation that shows the probability of occurrence of different magnitudes of flooding at a specific location, derived from historical hydrological data.
A graphical representation that shows the probability of exceeding a specified water surface elevation at a given location over time.

A graphical representation showing the expected frequency of exceedance of water surface elevations at a specific location over time.

A condition in which a structure remains intact and functional during seismic events without experiencing significant damage or collapse.
A condition where a structure's resistance to forces generated by ground shaking prevents it from undergoing failure, collapse, or excessive deformation.
The reliability of a slope to resist deformation and failure due to ground shaking.
A measure of a dam's ability to withstand earthquake-induced forces without sliding, overturning, or liquefaction.

A condition where structures resist failure or collapse under ground motion forces by satisfying strength, deformation, and displacement criteria derived from seismic analysis and design standards.

A limit imposed on the analysis to prevent structural elements from exceeding their ultimate capacity by representing their behavior as a maximum force or stress beyond which no further deformation occurs.
A standardized upper limit on the design strength for structural elements to ensure safety and reliability without overdesign.
A parameter that limits the maximum force or stress that a structural component can sustain before failure occurs.
A limit imposed on the design strength of a structural component to control deformation and prevent failure under extreme loading conditions.
A limit that restricts the maximum permissible yield strength for concrete to prevent brittle failure modes.
A parameter that limits the maximum strength of seismic actions used in structural design to prevent overestimation in seismic evaluations.
A limiting value imposed on the calculated shear strength of a structural component to prevent overestimation of its actual capacity.
A limit on the maximum flexural strength of a structural component determined by material properties and design criteria to ensure safety and performance.
Geotechnical failures caused by erosion and loss of soil matrix due to the migration of water through the material.
Stability failures occurring in channels or riverbanks due to excessive shear stresses induced by rapid hydraulic loading during high-flow events, leading to erosion and potential collapse.
Instabilities occurring in landslides or other geotechnical structures where shear strength is exceeded, leading to rapid mass movement and deformation.
A condition in embankment dams where excessive seepage undermines the structure's foundation, leading to erosion and potential collapse under saturated soil conditions.
Inclined or curvilinear slides that occur when a rock mass moves as a unit along a definite surface without internal distortion.
Erosion-induced landslides caused by the removal of sediment support in riverbeds, leading to channel instability and potential bank collapse.
Collapse of subaqueous dunes caused by the rapid movement of water through permeable sediments, triggered by high shear stresses during flood events.
A process in which the buoyant rise of fluidized particles within a sediment mass facilitates downslope movement under gravity.
A material composed of glass or ceramic particles bonded together under high pressure and temperature, exhibiting enhanced strength and durability.
A material that combines glass or ceramics with a high-pressure treatment to achieve enhanced mechanical strength and thermal stability.
A material composed of a compressed glass or ceramic layer sandwiched between two transparent plates to create a strong, impact-resistant glass/ceramic system.
A thermally sprayed composite material applied under high-pressure conditions to create a durable, adhesive bond between glass or ceramic substrates and a substrate surface.
A material that, when subjected to compressive stresses, exhibits a controllable and stable resistance to further deformation under sustained loading conditions.
A type of glass or ceramic material that has been subjected to controlled pressure during its manufacturing process to enhance its mechanical properties and resistance to fracture.

A construction material that incorporates glass or ceramic fragments within a compressed matrix to create a durable, transparent surface suitable for use in load-bearing structural elements without reinforcement.
A material composed of glass or ceramic particles enclosed within a pressure-resistant enclosure that ensures structural integrity and safety under high-pressure conditions.
A method that analyzes a structural model by applying lateral forces proportional to the structure's mass and distribution pattern to evaluate seismic demands.
A methodology that distributes seismic lateral forces horizontally across a building to simulate the effects of earthquake ground motion for structural analysis.
A method of determining seismic design forces by distributing a horizontal force to representative mass points in a building, scaled to the building's weight and seismic response spectrum.
A method where seismic forces are converted into horizontal components applied at the center of mass of a structure to simulate the dynamic effects of earthquakes.
A method used to estimate seismic forces by applying a horizontal force to a structure's mass distribution, accounting for both its weight and height-dependent damping effects.
A method to calculate seismic loads on a structure by applying horizontal forces proportional to its mass and distribution, representing the dynamic effects of ground motion.
A structural analysis method that distributes seismic forces as lateral loads equivalent to the inertial forces experienced during an earthquake to assess a building's response.
A method for approximating the seismic forces on a structure by distributing a horizontal load to simulate the effects of earthquake ground motion.

A structural component designed to distribute vertical loads primarily through bending, where its behavior is governed by flexural deformation rather than shear deformation.
A structural component that deforms primarily by bending under lateral seismic loads, with shear forces acting as secondary effects.
A structural element designed to resist seismic forces by deforming predominantly through bending, relying on its material's tensile and compressive strength rather than shear capacity.

A structural component formed by welding a T-shaped piece onto the end of a beam to provide a connection point for other structural elements.
A structural component that diverts and transfers water flow from a channel to a culvert or pipe by directing it horizontally into a vertical or sloping culvert inlet.
A structural element consisting of a horizontal steel plate welded perpendicularly to the end of a vertical steel column to distribute loads into multiple supporting columns.
A structural component interconnecting two or more header beams to transfer load laterally and distribute it evenly across the beam assembly.
A structural component inserted into the top of a column to distribute loads into a horizontal beam, also known as a header.
A structural component that transfers horizontal loads from the roof diaphragm to the vertical elements of the building's framing system.
A structural component that connects two main girders at an angle with a horizontal cross member to transfer loads and provide continuity between them.
A factor by which the torsional moment in a structural component is increased due to coupling between torsion and bending under lateral loading.

A factor applied to the torsional moment to account for the increase in moment due to coupling between translation and rotation in a structure under seismic loading.
An increase in seismic forces due to torsional coupling between the center of rigidity and the center of mass of a structure.

A bridge in which the deck is supported by vertical suspenders hung from main cables spanning between towers.
A structure where the deck is supported by cables suspended from towers, transferring load directly to the foundations without intermediate piers.
A structural system that spans large waterways or valleys using cables suspended from towers to carry road or rail traffic across.
A bridge supported by cables that hang from towers and transmit the weight of the roadway directly to anchorages at either end.
Method for calculating wind loads on structural components by treating one end of the member as fully restrained, allowing for the determination of maximum stresses under lateral wind pressure.
A method for determining the shear forces and moments at the base of a structure by assuming it is fixed and analyzing the resulting internal forces and moments.
A method for estimating reaction forces at a structural support by assuming it to be completely fixed and unable to translate or rotate in any direction.
Procedures where the structure's base is assumed to remain fixed and immobile during analysis, neglecting foundation deformations.
Procedures used to estimate a building's fundamental period and spectral response by analyzing observed response data, assuming the base of the structure remains fixed during an earthquake.

Methods where structures are assumed to be completely restrained at their base, which may overestimate or underestimate actual behavior depending on foundation conditions.
A force that varies linearly along one axis, with distinct values at two points and a uniform slope connecting them, applied to a structure to simulate loading conditions.

A force applied over a cross-section that varies linearly along the width of the member.

The maximum axial load at which a structural column will fail due to elastic instability under compressive loading.

The maximum compressive force at which a structural component undergoes sudden lateral deflection due to its inherent instability, without considering material yielding.
The lowest load at which an axially compressed structural member can no longer maintain its original shape under small additional loads due to lateral instability.

The maximum axial compressive load at which an idealized column, without considering imperfections or residual stresses, loses its ability to support a load due to buckling while remaining within its elastic range.

A zone within approximately 10 km of a fault where structures may experience significant velocity pulses due to an approaching fault rupture.
A zone adjacent to a fault where ground motion is characterized by direct rupture, fling, and forward directivity effects that deviate from the standard effective source radius assumption.
A zone adjacent to an active fault where the seismic motion can include forward directivity and fling effects, potentially causing high ground accelerations and velocity pulses.

Monetary damages incurred by infrastructure owners due to physical damage or disruption of assets in an earthquake.

Financial costs incurred due to damage or destruction of structures, including repair and replacement expenses.
Quantitative damages directly incurred by individuals or businesses due to the destruction of assets caused by a natural disaster.

Monetary damages resulting from the immediate financial impact of an earthquake on physical infrastructure and properties.
Monetary damages to property and infrastructure resulting from a natural hazard event, calculated by assessing the repair or replacement costs of damaged elements.

Approximate methods that estimate permanent displacement of soil slopes by partitioning the driving and resisting forces on a sliding block subject to earthquake loading to assess stability.
Analytical techniques that estimate seismic displacements by assuming a rigid block on a friction surface responding to ground motion.

A numerical approach that simulates the behavior of a rigid block sliding down an inclined plane under seismic loading by discretizing the acceleration-time history and calculating the cumulative displacement.
Forces exerted by water in motion on a structure due to currents, waves, or other fluid dynamics, which can vary with time and location.

Forces exerted on a structure by water in motion, arising from wave action, currents, and other fluid dynamics.

Forces exerted on a structure due to the movement of water.
Forces exerted on a structure by the dynamic interaction between water and its surrounding environment, such as waves and currents.
Forces exerted on a structure due to the dynamic motion of water against its surface during flood events.
Forces exerted on a structure by water movement during a flood event, calculated based on the water's velocity and density.
A reversible change in shape or length of a material under load, where it returns to its original dimensions upon unloading.
A reversible change in shape or size of a material that occurs under load, returning to its original state once the load is removed.
A deformation that occurs within a material's elastic range where stress is directly proportional to strain, and the material returns to its original shape when unloaded.
A change in shape or dimension of a material that returns to its original state when the applied load is removed.
A temporary change in shape or dimensions of a structural member that disappears upon removal of applied loads and can be fully recovered after the loads are removed.
A deformation that occurs without permanent changes to the material's properties when stresses are removed.
A change in shape or size of a material under load that disappears when the load is removed, without permanent damage occurring.
A response where the material returns to its original shape after the removal of applied loads, without permanent damage.

Fine-grained sediment that accumulates beneath the mouth of a river where turbidity currents deposit material during low-flow conditions.

Fine-grained sediment deposited at the base of a delta by sediment-laden turbidity currents and settling processes.

Specified parameters at the ends of a structural member that define the restraints and interactions influencing its behavior during analysis.
Specifications that define the behavior of a structural model at its limits, such as fixed supports or hinges, which constrain or allow movement to simulate real-world restraints.
Constraints imposed on the behavior of a structural component at its ends or interfaces to define the constraints on its displacement, rotation, or forces during analysis.
Constraints imposed on a structural model at its points of support to simulate the actual restraints provided by the foundation or supports.

Specifications that dictate how a structural element interacts with adjacent materials or supports, influencing its behavior and response under load.
Specified conditions at the limits of a material domain that define the constraints and external forces acting on the structure.
Specifications that define the constraints or requirements at the limits of a structural model, establishing the conditions under which the structure interacts with its external environment.

A structural analysis approach that determines lateral forces on diaphragm components by resolving vertical reactions from individual columns into horizontal shear components.
Forces applied to a structure during its design life that must be considered for ensuring structural safety and performance.

Forces or effects acting on a structure, including static and dynamic forces, that induce internal stresses and deformation, necessitating structural design to ensure safety and performance under service and extreme conditions.
External forces applied to a structure that it must resist during its service life.

External forces or pressures acting on a structure that cause it to resist and maintain its stability.
Forces or effects applied to a structural component that cause internal stresses and deformations, potentially leading to failure or instability.
Forces, moments, and other actions applied to a structural component or system that result in stresses, deformations, or reactions.
Mechanisms exerting forces on an object with the potential to cause failure or damage.
A statistical measure representing the variability of change in internal energy values within a system.

A measure of the variability of the uncertainty in the estimation of resistance factor values.

A curve that describes the change in grade along a roadway to ensure a gradual transition between two adjacent tangent sections.
A portion of a highway where the grade changes progressively from one slope to another to provide a smooth transition in elevation.
A segment in a road's alignment where the road transitions between two different grades.
The particle size at which 90% of the material in a sample is finer by mass.
The particle size at which 90% of a filter material's mass is finer, calculated by linear interpolation between sieves.
The diameter of a grain size distribution curve at which 90% of the particles are smaller, representing the smallest size for particles in the coarsest 10%.

A specified equation that sums individual loads multiplied by their respective load factors to determine the total design load effect for structural analysis.

A factor applied to the ultimate strength of a structural component to determine the strength at first yield or onset of significant inelastic deformation.
A factor applied to the yield strength of reinforcing steel to account for the enhancement of its yield stress during loading due to strain hardening effects.
A factor that adjusts the yield strength of concrete to account for its actual ability to sustain higher loads beyond its nominal yield point due to material properties and testing conditions.
A factor applied to the theoretical strength of a material to account for the influence of strain hardening on its actual stress-strain behavior under loading.
A factor applied to the theoretical strength of a material to account for its actual measured strength in a test.
A factor applied to the yield strength of a structural component to account for the increased resistance that develops beyond initial yield due to strain hardening.
A non-destructive evaluation technique used to assess material properties without altering the structure or component under inspection.
A standardized evaluation method used to judge the acceptability of flaws in structural components without requiring their removal from service.
A method of assessing structural integrity without causing damage or altering the structure.
A method used to examine the internal structure of materials without causing damage.
A technique that evaluates the internal integrity of structural components without requiring destructive testing.
Non-Destructive Evaluation is a method used to assess the integrity of structural components without causing damage or altering their properties.
A non-destructive evaluation technique used to assess the condition and integrity of structural components without causing damage.
Non-destructive evaluation techniques that assess material properties without causing damage.
System of bearings designed to support a structure by allowing adjustment and movement through the use of two distinct and independent bearing pads.
Two bearings installed at each end of a bridge girder to accommodate longitudinal movement and reduce friction by allowing the girder to move independently of the pier.
Two rollers or thrust surfaces that support and guide a rotating component while accommodating axial displacement.
A system of supports where a vehicle rests on two sets of wheels, enabling independent movement of each axle to improve traction and stability under load.
Supporting structures that allow a bridge deck to move horizontally and rotate vertically under temperature changes and loads.
Two bearings placed side by side to support the same end of a bridge girder, sharing the load and providing redundancy and flexibility in case of bearing failure.

A structural feature consisting of two independent bearing surfaces provided to support a column and distribute its load across a wider area, allowing for potential removal and replacement of one bearing while the column remains in service.
A system in which two bearings, one located above the other, are used to support a structural member, distributing the load and accommodating structural movement.
A central zone of uncrushed concrete surrounded by transverse reinforcement that remains intact and resists axial loads in a concrete column.
A component within a structural wall where the vertical reinforcement is enclosed within concrete to resist axial loads while allowing the wall to effectively transfer lateral forces.
A concrete core surrounded by structural steel elements that resist lateral loads while allowing the concrete to expand under compressive stresses.
A compressive or tensile region within a structural member where concrete is surrounded by longitudinal and transverse reinforcement to resist cracking and failure.
A central portion of a pier or column that remains enclosed within a concrete wall to resist applied loads and transfer forces to the foundation.
A mass of concrete surrounded and compacted by steel reinforcement, designed to resist high lateral pressures and prevent bursting under loading.
The portion of a pile that is entirely surrounded by densified soil or grout, designed to resist axial loads by direct bearing on the surrounding material.
A segment of a dam's concrete structure surrounded by steel mesh and grout injection to resist uplift pressure and improve stability.
Modeling elements that represent the stiffness of soil beneath a structural foundation by simulating it as a series of interconnected vertical springs.
Mechanisms that simulate soil resistance by translating horizontal displacements into vertical forces to stabilize piles against lateral loads.
Structures that transmit loads into the soil by resisting vertical displacement through compression or shear.
Representation of the soil resistance against foundation movement as discrete springs that act in the vertical direction to simulate the soil's stiffness and load-carrying capacity.
Elements that resist foundation movement in a purely vertical direction through soil stiffness.
Mechanisms that simulate soil resistance against structural movements by modeling soil stiffness as linear springs oriented perpendicular to the structural base.
Structural elements that simulate soil resistance by providing vertical reaction forces in foundation models.
Modeling elements that simulate the resistance of soil as it supports and interacts with structural foundations or retaining walls under vertical loading.
The depth of water below the control structure that determines the downstream water surface elevation and influences the operation and design of hydraulic structures.
The elevation of the water surface at the downstream end of a hydraulic structure that influences the depth and flow conditions within the channel.
A body of water at the downstream end of a channel or structure that restricts the flow of water from upstream and influences the water surface elevation for hydraulic calculations.
The elevation or depth of water at the downstream end of a channel or structure that affects the submergence and flow characteristics of the upstream water.
The depth of water downstream of a hydraulic structure against which a dam or weir must operate.
The depth of water downstream from a structure that influences the flow and submergence conditions affecting the operation of a dam.
The depth of water at the downstream end of a channel or structure that affects the water surface profile and flow conditions upstream.
The elevation of water in a stream or channel immediately downstream of a dam or structure that influences the pool elevation and must be considered in the design of flood protection measures.
A coefficient that reduces the design forces by accounting for the inherent ductility and overstrength of a structural system's components.
A factor that reduces the design base shear force for a structure by accounting for its inherent ability to dissipate seismic energy through inelastic deformation.
A factor applied to increase the design forces for structural components to account for energy dissipation during seismic response.
A factor applied to reduce the design forces for a structural component to account for its ability to dissipate energy through inelastic deformation during seismic shaking.
A coefficient applied to reduce the design seismic forces for structures that dissipate energy through inelastic deformation under seismic loading.
A factor applied to reduce the design seismic forces in a structure by accounting for the inherent energy dissipation and deformation capacity of the structural system.
A multiplier applied to the design forces to reduce the seismic demands on structural components by accounting for the inelastic deformation capacity of the structure.
A factor that reduces the design forces for a structural system based on its ability to dissipate energy through ductile behavior under seismic loading.
A statistical measure representing the dispersion among different earthquake ground motion recordings used in structural analysis.
A coefficient representing the statistical dispersion among seismic response spectra derived from different ground motion records at a specific site.

A statistical parameter representing the standard deviation of response quantities across different seismic ground motion records used in structural analysis, reflecting inherent uncertainty in ground motion selection.

A statistical measure quantifying the dispersion in response quantities between different ground motion records with the same magnitude and distance, used to assess the uncertainty in analytical predictions.
A statistical measure quantifying the dispersion in structural response due to differences between individual ground motion records used in analysis.

A statistical parameter representing the variability in response quantities across different earthquake ground motions, quantified as the standard deviation of the ratio of individual responses to the mean response.
A statistical measure representing the inherent variability between ground motion records due to differences in source, path, and site effects.
A statistical parameter used to quantify the variability in ground motion intensities between different earthquake records, essential for assessing structural response uncertainty.
Linear elastic elements that model soil resistance by resisting vertical movement proportionally to displacement without accounting for mutual interaction between adjacent springs.
Linear elements that model soil resistance to vertical loads by simulating a discrete, point-wise relationship between surface pressure and displacement.
A mathematical model that represents the soil reaction beneath a foundation as a series of independent, linearly elastic springs, each resisting vertical displacement in proportion to its deflection.
Elements representing the soil's resistance to foundation movement by providing a reaction proportional to displacement at each point of contact.
A theoretical model representing soil resistance as independent linear springs that react against footing displacements without interaction between adjacent springs.
A simple model of soil support represented by discrete elastic springs thatdeflect proportionally to the applied load and are used to simulate soil reaction in foundation analysis.
Elastic supports that provide independent resistance to vertical displacement, simulating soil reactions through a linear relationship between pressure and settlement.
A model representing soil resistance as a series of independent elastic springs that provide linear resistance proportional to the displacement they undergo.
A computational technique that simulates a structural component's dynamic behavior by applying a ground motion's acceleration history directly to its mass matrix.
A technique that determines structural behavior by integrating dynamic forces and displacements over time, simulating the actual response under seismic loading.
A method that calculates a structure's seismic response by integrating dynamic equations of motion over time using ground motion accelerograms to predict deformations, forces, and failure potential.
A procedure that calculates the dynamic behavior of a structure by directly integrating the time-varying forces from an earthquake ground motion record into the equations of motion.
A method that calculates dynamic response by applying time-dependent ground motions to determine structural behavior under seismic loading.
It is a method that calculates the seismic response of a structure by incrementally solving the equations of motion over time using ground motion time histories.
A computational method that determines the structural response by directly solving the equations of motion using a time-dependent loading history.
A computational method that calculates the structural response by directly integrating the dynamic equations of motion over time using specified ground motion histories.
A structural system composed of multiple layers of materials designed to distribute and dissipate earthquake forces by altering their dynamic characteristics.
A construction method where multiple layers of concrete are placed and cured sequentially to achieve a thick structural component.
A structural system consisting of multiple layers of materials with varying mechanical properties and thicknesses to achieve desired performance and behavior under load.
A structural system where multiple layers of materials, such as concrete and steel, are mechanically bonded together to act as a single unit under load.
A construction method where multiple layers of materials are applied sequentially to a surface to achieve specific performance characteristics, durability, and aesthetics.
A structural system composed of multiple layers of materials or components working together to provide strength, stability, and energy dissipation under seismic loading.
A structural system composed of multiple layers of materials, each designed to distribute and resist imposed loads in a coordinated manner.
A structural material composed of multiple layers of different materials with varying characteristics, designed to work together to enhance the overall performance and durability of the pavement.
A component used to determine the seismic response modification factor (R) of a structural system by providing the median response of a group of similar elements subjected to dynamic loading.
A component whose relative displacement or deformation is measured to determine the response of another component under applied loads or environmental changes.
A component whose acceleration response spectrum or other dynamic properties are used to scale the response of a seismic design force-resisting system for design purposes.
A structural or nonstructural element whose response is used to quantify the performance of other components under seismic loading.
It is the component upon which the other components are referenced and aligned.
A structural component whose response is used to establish the baseline for comparisons and adjustments in seismic design and analysis.
The portion of a structural component that is assumed to remain intact and undamaged under load, providing a benchmark for evaluating deformation and force distributions in the damaged component.
A seismic ground motion component derived from a specific direction of earthquake shaking to which other components are compared for evaluating response in structures.
The vertical distance between the top of concrete pavement and a reference plane established by a line tangent to the lowest point of the vertical curve.
The upward curvature specified in design to compensate for the downward deflection under full service load, ensuring a flat deck surface.
A vertical curve intentionally introduced in a concrete bridge deck to counteract differential shrinkage and ensure a flat surface during service.
The vertical distance between the undeflected centerline of a bridge deck and the straight line connecting its supports, used to offset the deflection under service loads and ensure proper drainage.
The vertical curvature intentionally introduced into a bridge deck to counteract the deflection under full service loads and maintain a flat surface.

The vertical distance between the elevation of the road surface at a bridge and the straight-line distance between the support elevations, calculated to maintain the desired superstructure profile during construction.
The initial upward curve intentionally introduced into the concrete deck surface during construction to compensate for dead and live load deflections and ensure a flat riding surface over time.
The initial curvature intentionally introduced into a bridge deck during construction to ensure that it achieves the desired horizontal alignment after the concrete hardens and settles.
The property of a concrete mixture that allows it to be easily compacted and smoothed during placement and finishing operations to achieve a high-quality surface.
A property of concrete that determines its capability to achieve a smooth, dense, and durable surface when properly placed, consolidated, and finished.
The property of a concrete surface that determines its ability to accept and retain a decorative finish without requiring extensive additional preparation or repairs.
The property of a concrete surface that allows for a smooth and even application of a desired surface finish without excessive effort during the final stages of placement and compaction.
It is the ability for a concrete surface to be easily and uniformly finished to the desired texture or smoothness without an excessive amount of labor or skill.
The property of a concrete mix that allows it to achieve a smooth and uniform surface under finishing operations such as troweling or floating.
The property of a bituminous mixture that allows the surface to be smoothed and compacted during construction to achieve a dense, uniform layer.
The characteristic of a concrete surface that indicates its ability to be properly finished to achieve the desired texture and appearance.
The ability of a structural member to sustain deformation beyond its elastic limit by redistributing stress through localized bending before complete failure occurs.

It is the load-carrying capacity at which a structural component experiences significant deformation under compressive stress, transitioning from elastic to plastic behavior without additional cross-sectional hardening.

The ultimate load-carrying capacity of a structural member when it undergoes lateral deflections beyond its elastic limit due to bending stresses, causing a loss of load-carrying capacity in localized areas.

A structural property representing the maximum stress at which a component will sustain significant deformation without loss of load-carrying capacity due to local plate instability under cyclic loading.
The maximum stress a steel member can sustain before its cross-section deforms plastically due to an instability localized within its slender elements.
The capacity of a structural member to sustain deformation beyond its elastic limit through localized buckling before loss of load-carrying ability occurs.
The capability of a structural element to sustain deformation beyond its elastic limit due to localized buckling effects.
The capacity of a compression member to resist buckling beyond its elastic limit, determined by strain hardening effects and post-buckling behavior.
A condition where the strains in adjacent structural elements are consistent with their relative displacements and interactions under applied loads.
A condition requiring that the deformations of interconnected structural elements must be compatible to maintain structural integrity without inducing discontinuities or excessive stresses.
A condition requiring that the calculated displacements and rotations at the ends of structural components match to ensure continuity and consistency in their interaction.
A condition in structural analysis where the displacements at the interface of adjacent structural components are equal to maintain continuity of movement.
A condition requiring that the strains in a structure adjust such that adjacent elements maintain continuity and fit together without gaps or overlaps.
A condition where the displacements and strains in adjacent structural elements are consistent and continuous, ensuring structural integrity and load distribution.
The requirement that all structural components must deform in a manner that maintains continuity and avoids separation when subjected to loads.
A condition in structural analysis where the deformations of connected elements match to ensure equilibrium and satisfy the boundary conditions.
Beams that form the outer boundary of a bridge deck and support it while carrying traffic loads.
The structural members located along the outer edges of a bridge that span between piers and support the bridge deck and superstructure.
Beams that carry deck loads between the supports at the outer edge of the bridge.
Beams located on the outer edges of a bridge that carry the loads from the deck and distribute them to the substructures.
Girders located at the edges of a bridge that do not have interior girders to transfer loads to.
Beams that support the deck at the outer edges of a bridge and transfer loads to the bridge's substructure.
Girders located along the outer edges of a bridge deck that directly support the deck and distribute loads to the substructure.
The primary longitudinal members that support and distribute loads to the substructure at the outer edges of a bridge deck.

A measure of the variability in the strength of a structural component that incorporates uncertainties from all contributing sources, including material properties, geometric deviations, and load effects, to assess the likelihood of collapse under seismic loading.
A coefficient representing the combined influence of uncertainties in material properties, construction quality, and other structural parameters on the overall seismic performance of a building.
A statistical parameter representing the combined uncertainty in structural response due to both modeling errors and randomness inherent in material properties and load variations.
A measure representing the combined uncertainty in structural collapse due to all sources, including load and resistance factors, as calculated using first-order reliability methods.
A statistical measure quantifying the combined uncertainties in material strength and applied loads within a structural system to assess its likelihood of collapse under seismic loading.
A statistical parameter representing the combined variability and uncertainty in seismic demand and structural capacity that affects the likelihood of structural collapse.

A parameter representing the combined uncertainty in structural performance due to all sources, including material properties, structural analysis, and load estimation, used to assess the probability of total system collapse under seismic loading.
The uncertainty associated with the collapse probability of a structural system, considering the combined effects of modeling assumptions and structural variability.
Narrow tunnels excavated ahead of the main tunnel to guide and stabilize the construction process and provide access for drilling and blasting operations.
Horizontal access tunnels driven ahead of main tunnels to assess rock mass conditions, locate faults, and establish surface benchmarks for alignment accuracy.
Tunnels excavated in front of the primary tunnel to prepare for and guide the construction of the main tunnel.
Tunnels excavated ahead of the main tunnel to provide support for the overlying strata and facilitate the removal of ground during the construction of the main tunnel.
Tunnels constructed ahead of the main excavation to guide and support the placement of the tunnel boring machine (TBM) and to monitor ground conditions.
Small-diameter openings excavated ahead of the main excavation to provide advance support, information, and guidance for the primary tunneling operations.
Underground passages excavated ahead of the main tunnel to serve as temporary support and guide for the construction machinery during the driving of large tunnels.
Narrow, exploratory tunnels driven along the proposed alignment of a main tunnel to test ground conditions, locate geological features, and adjust the design before full-scale excavation.
A flow condition where the depth of water changes slowly along the channel in response to changes in channel geometry or bed slope, and the flow remains constant over time.
A condition where the depth and velocity of flow change slowly along a channel due to friction and slope variations, without unsteady effects or rapid changes in depth.
A flow condition where the water surface profile changes slowly over time and space with constant discharge through a channel.
A flow condition where depth gradually changes along a channel due to friction and gravity, with constant discharge over time.
A flow condition where the depth changes gradually along the channel due to a balance between friction, pressure, and gravity forces while maintaining constant discharge over time.
A flow condition where the depth varies along the channel over a distance due to changes in bed slope, channel geometry, or other factors while maintaining a constant discharge.
A flow condition where the water surface profile changes gradually over time due to variations in channel geometry, roughness, and slope, but the discharge remains steady.
A condition where the flow depth and velocity change gradually along the channel due to steady flow and gentle slope variations.
The degree to which a design permits efficient and safe construction practices while adhering to cost and schedule constraints.
A qualitative assessment of how readily a structure can be built, considering the feasibility and practicality of the proposed design based on available construction methods and technologies.
The degree to which a design can be efficiently and safely executed during construction, considering practical constraints and potential impacts on the buildability of a project.
The degree to which a structural design can be effectively and efficiently built using conventional construction methods and materials without requiring unusual or impractical measures.
It is the extent to which a structural design can be economically erected with currently available materials and construction techniques.
The degree to which a building can be efficiently and economically erected in its intended location, considering the materials, methods, and equipment available.
The degree to which a structural design can be realistically implemented during construction, considering practical limitations and feasibility.

The degree to which a design can be effectively realized during the construction phase, considering practical considerations of material availability, sequence of operations, and contractor experience.
A structural component that relies solely on physical interference or engagement between mating surfaces to resist separation under applied loads without the use of adhesive materials.
A design element that secures formwork panels together by interlocking parts without the use of fasteners, relying on mechanical force to maintain positioning and alignment.
A structural component designed to restrict relative movement between two building elements by interlocking or engaging them mechanically.
A device that physically interlocks two or more parts to resist separation under load, such as interlocking tabs on a connector.

A geometric design that engages and resists movement between adjacent concrete deck segments by relying solely on the shape and form of the concrete without the use of additional mechanical fasteners.
A structural component designed to prevent movement between two elements without relying solely on adhesive bonding, capable of transferring mechanical stress and resisting relative displacement.
A structural component that secures concrete forms together through physical interconnection without reliance on adhesive or mechanical fasteners.
A structural component that engages and restrains adjoining pieces of concrete through physical interaction, transferring loads and preventing relative movement without relying on adhesive bonding.
The ratio of the area of longitudinal reinforcement to the gross cross-sectional area of the concrete element.
The ratio of the cross-sectional area of reinforcing steel to the area of concrete in a structural element, expressed as a percentage, that influences its strength and behavior under load.
The ratio of the area of reinforcing steel to the gross concrete area in a structural member.
The ratio of the area of steel reinforcement to the gross area of concrete in a structural member, calculated to ensure adequate strength and ductility.
The fraction of the cross-sectional area of steel bars to the total gross concrete area within a structural member.
The ratio of the cross-sectional area of reinforcing steel to the gross cross-sectional area of concrete in a structural member.
The proportion of steel reinforcement area relative to the concrete cross-sectional area in a structural member.
The ratio of the cross-sectional area of the steel reinforcement to the gross cross-sectional area of the concrete in a structural member, expressed as a percentage.
Cavities within concrete structural components that have not been fully filled with grout during the installation process.
Spaces within concrete filled with cementitious material that are not fully occupied, potentially leading to structural deficiencies.
Hollow spaces in grouted structural joints where cementitious material did not fully fill the space during the installation process.
Sealed, enclosed spaces within precast concrete components filled with grout that may be partially or fully void of grout material due to inadequate filling techniques.
Cavities left in a concrete structure due to improper placement or inadequate consolidation of grout during repairs or installations.
Hollow spaces that form within concrete structural elements due to the failure of injected grout to completely fill voids around embedded steel reinforcement.
Cavities within concrete-filled structural components that develop due to insufficient grout placement, potentially compromising structural integrity.
Spaces within the concrete that are not filled with grout during the post-tensioning tendon installation process.
A professional with a license to practice structural design, ensuring compliance with codes and standards.
A licensed engineer or architect responsible for signing and sealing construction documents to verify compliance with building codes and standards.
A professional who is licensed and qualified to prepare, sign, and seal design documents for structural engineering projects.
A licensed architect or engineer who prepares or seals drawings and documents for structural projects that are subject to jurisdictional review.
A licensed architect or engineer who has been designated to sign and seal construction documents, ensuring their accuracy and compliance with building codes.
A licensed architect or engineer who has been approved by the state board to sign and seal structural plans and specifications.
A licensed engineer or architect who has met the qualifications and requirements set forth by the licensing authority to provide professional services related to structural design and engineering.
A licensed engineer or architect responsible for the design and review of structural elements to ensure they meet safety and performance standards.
A process that uses definite values for all relevant parameters to calculate the force or moment demands acting on structural components.
A method for assessing structural behavior where standardized ground motion records are applied to a model to predict maximum response quantities without accounting for ground motion variability.

A method that predicts the response of a structure to a prescribed earthquake ground motion by calculating the maximum demand on structural components without considering probabilistic or statistical variations.
A method that calculates structural response using predefined excitations and material properties without accounting for probabilistic variations in input parameters.
A methodology that evaluates structural response under extreme loading by considering only the characteristic strengths and demands, without incorporating probability or variability.

A method of assessing structural response to seismic loading by assuming that ground motion effects can be represented by a single, specific, and well-defined set of ground motion parameters to determine maximum demands on structural components.
A method that calculates structural response using predefined force levels and material properties without considering probabilistic variation in load or resistance.
A method that estimates earthquake effects by considering the maximum response from a single, predefined ground motion scenario without probabilistic variation.
A wall designed to resist seismic forces by resisting out-of-plane bending and shear, thereby providing stability to adjacent concrete diaphragms.
A structural wall that meets specific height-to-length ratios and seismic force requirements to act as a seismic force-resisting element within a compliant wood-sheathed wall panel system.

A structural element that spans between intersecting walls to transfer seismic forces from the diaphragm to the lateral force-resisting system by developing a shear resistance equal to the lesser of 50% of the diaphragm shear or the shear capacity of the wall.
A wall that is perpendicular to the exterior wall it braces and has sufficient stiffness to limit the deflection of that exterior wall under lateral loads.
A structural element perpendicular to the diaphragm that enhances its capacity to resist seismic forces by distributing loads and providing additional lateral support.
A structural element designed to resist seismic forces in two orthogonal directions by providing stiffness and strength through its connection and interaction with adjacent walls.

A wall that, when utilized as a shear wall or coupled with adjacent shear walls, satisfies the proportion and spacing requirements to effectively distribute and resist seismic forces within a wood-sheathed wood-frame structure.
A wall that meets specific height, length, and spacing requirements to function as a substitute for structural wood panel shear walls in a structural panel system.
A tool that estimates the travel time contours for major ground motions in a specific frequency band, aiding in the design and analysis of structural components.
A methodology that calculates a site-specific ground motion response spectrum by mapping seismic wave travel times onto a map and deriving the resulting ground motion intensity at a given location.
A tool that estimates seismic ground motion parameters at specific arrival times for different earthquake magnitudes and distances.
A statistical model that estimates the probability of a ground motion exceeding a specified level at a specified hazard level by integrating spectral acceleration values over a range of frequencies.

An analytical tool used to estimate the variation in seismic energy distribution across a fault surface by calculating the time-dependent radiation pattern based on fault geometry and rupture propagation.
A model that utilizes seismic wave propagation characteristics to estimate the arrival times of ground motions at specific locations relative to an earthquake's source.
A tool that estimates the time variation of ground motion parameters along specific paths from an earthquake source based on empirical relationships between distance and intensity.

A tool that calculates the expected peak ground motion values for a given earthquake magnitude and distance, incorporating site-specific soil conditions and geological factors to predict ground shaking intensity.
A structural component that anchors the pipe at one end while allowing the other end to pivot and adjust vertically to accommodate thermal movement and settlement.
A structural component that provides lateral bracing for a pipe by forming an L-shaped frame to resist lateral displacement while allowing vertical movement.
A structural component that anchors and supports a pipe laterally without utilizing vertical reactions, designed to maintain alignment and prevent lateral movement under load.
A structural component designed to bear the weight of a buried pipe by extending horizontally from the ground surface without requiring lateral bracing.
A structural component that provides lateral support and stability for a pipe by resisting horizontal loads through its embedded base without requiring additional bracing.
A structure designed to brace and stabilize the end of a pipe by resisting its lateral and vertical displacement through rigid connection to a foundation.
A structural element that extends horizontally from a wall or pier to provide lateral support and resist horizontal loads on a buried pipe by transferring them directly into the supporting structure.
A structural component that extends horizontally from a wall to support a pipe by resisting its vertical load and transferring it to the foundation below.
A measure of the structural stiffness derived by dividing the applied load by the total deformation at that load level, reflecting the behavior of a structure between its yield and peak capacities.
The ratio of the initial yield strength to the maximum stress at fracture in a tensile test, representing the material's stiffness up to yield.
A measure of the structural stiffness determined by the ratio of the shear force to the shear displacement at a specific point on the load-displacement curve.

A quantity derived by dividing the stress at a given strain by the secant of the angle between the load-deformation curve and the strain axis at that point, representing the slope of a line connecting the origin to the point on the curve.
The stiffness derived from the slope of the secant line connecting the origin to a point on the stress-strain curve of a material under load.
The ratio of the yield strength to the yield displacement of a structural component, representing its stiffness up to the yield point under monotonic loading.
The ratio of the peak moment to the peak rotation in a component's moment-rotation relationship, used to assess its post-yield behavior.
The ratio of the actual force to the corresponding displacement in a structural component, calculated along the secant line connecting the origin to a point on its force-displacement curve.
A phenomenon where the concurrent application of group and cyclic loads results in cumulative damage to concrete, enhancing durability concerns.
A phenomenon where cyclic loading, such as that induced by wave action, interacts with the structural response to produce cumulative damage over time.

A phenomenon where the cumulative impact of repetitive loads, either as part of a group or in a cyclic pattern, can result in a deformation that is greater than the sum of their individual effects under static loading.

A phenomenon wherein repeated cyclic loading, in combination with group effects such as loading history and cumulative damage, leads to a progressive degradation of structural performance and function beyond the predictions based on static or linear fatigue analysis alone.
A phenomenon in which repeated and cyclic loading of a pile group causes greater settlement than an equivalent single static load due to cumulative soil compression and densification.
An interaction in which two different types of loading, specifically group and cyclic loading, are applied concurrently to a structure, potentially leading to cumulative damage or altered behavior.
A phenomenon where the combined impact of group and cyclic loading interactions affects the structural response, potentially altering load distribution and stress patterns within the system.

The phenomenon where simultaneous application of group loading and cyclic loading on a pile group results in a stress distribution that is not linearly additive, necessitating a more complex analysis to determine its impact on pile response and capacity.
Internal forces developed within a structure to resist imposed deformations and maintain equilibrium under applied loads.
Forces exerted by adjacent structures to resist the movement of a structure constrained by a floor joint or restraint.
Forces exerted by surrounding rock or concrete to prevent movement or deformation of a structural component in a tunnel.
Forces that oppose the outward thrust of a structure's substructure by providing lateral resistance to maintain stability.
Forces that resist the movement of a constrained object and act opposite to the direction of its intended motion.
Forces that prevent a body from moving in a particular direction by opposing its tendency to move or rotate.
Forces applied to a pile to resist movement during driving by engaging with a driving shoe and a reaction beam.
Component forces that resist movement along a failure plane due to the friction between the soil mass and any rigid structures in contact.
A floating structure equipped with hydraulic legs that can be extended to raise the barge above water for dredging or support operations.
A floating platform that supports a derrick or rig by raising it above the water level through hydraulic jacks.
A marine structure that supports drilling operations by raising itself onto the seabed using hydraulic jacks.
A floating platform that elevates itself above the water by hydraulically extending legs into the seabed to support offshore drilling and construction operations.
A vessel equipped with hydraulic jacks that raise it off the seabed to stabilize and support a taller structure during construction or maintenance operations.
A structure consisting of a floating platform supported by legs that can be raised or lowered to maintain its position in shallow water by adjusting its draft.
A floating platform that supports large cranes and can be raised or lowered by hydraulic jacks to adjust its elevation.
A structure capable of supporting an offshore platform by elevating its legs above the seabed using hydraulic jacks.
A source of material excavated from a designated area for use in constructing fill or embankments.
A site where material is extracted for use as fill in embankments or other structures.
A designated area from which soil or rock is excavated to create borrow material for filling or embankment construction.
A location from which soil or rock is excavated and transported to a construction site for use as fill material.
A designated excavation area from which material is extracted to replenish or construct dams, levees, or other structures.
A depression excavated in a suitable location to obtain material for constructing fill embankments or other structures.
A construction site excavation where material is extracted for use as fill in another location.
A site from which excavated material is obtained and transported to build up or fill in low-lying areas, dredged channels, or other waterways.

A condition wherein the soil beneath a structural element exhibits mechanical properties that allow it to deform in response to applied loads, thereby influencing the overall structural behavior and possibly necessitating a detailed analysis to account for these effects.
A condition where the soil beneath a structure allows it to move or settle unevenly under load, modifying the stress distribution and potentially affecting structural performance.
A condition where the soil beneath a structure does not provide uniform support, leading to differential settlement and potential structural deformation.
A condition where the subgrade or soil beneath the foundation can deform or settle under applied loads, affecting structure stability.
The phenomenon where a foundation's stiffness and displacement characteristics influence the structural response to applied loads.
A property of the soil that allows it to deform under the applied load, influencing the distribution and magnitude of stresses in the foundation system.
It refers to the ability of a structure's base to deform under load, impacting its stability and load distribution.
A condition where the underlying soil or rock can deform under applied loads, influencing the structural response to loading.
A space beneath a residential structure, typically used for utilities and access, that is less than 24 inches in height and is ventilated to prevent moisture accumulation.
A shallow space beneath a home's living area, open to the exterior, used for utilities and access but not intended for habitable living.
A covered area, typically between the ground and the first floor, used to support the house and provide access for utilities and maintenance.
A shallow foundation system where the floor rests on a concrete slab supported by posts set into the ground without full ground contact beneath.
A void space beneath a building's first floor that is used for utility access and allows air circulation but is not an accessible habitable space.
A confined space beneath a building, accessed by stairs or a door and used for utility access and foundation support.
A space beneath a building where the height is less than the height of a finished floor, used to allow access to utilities or for ventilation and drainage purposes.
A shallow, uninhabitable area beneath a structure that provides access for utilities and allows air circulation.
The moment at which a structural member reaches its ultimate capacity under bending, signifying the point where it can no longer sustain additional loading before failure occurs.
The moment at which a structural member reaches its maximum resistance to bending before exhibiting significant cracking or deformation.
The resistance a structural component exhibits against applied moments before it reaches its ultimate deformation capacity.
The maximum moment a structural component can resist before it undergoes significant flexural failure.
The internal moment capacity a structural component can sustain before exceeding its flexural failure limit.
