The period during which an aquatic herbicide is applied to control underwater plants in a water body.
The period during which an herbicide is applied to control weeds in a vineyard.
The period during which a pesticide is applied to a crop or area to control pests and prevent damage.
The period during which a pesticide is applied to a target crop to control specific pests, typically influenced by climatic and agricultural conditions.
The period during which a pesticide is applied to crops to control pests or diseases.
The period in which irrigation water is distributed to crops due to their specific water requirements for growth and development.
Structural supports that allow the center span of a three-span continuous girder bridge to rotate freely while maintaining continuity at the abutments.
Structural supports that pivot on vertical curved surfaces to accommodate horizontal movements and reduce friction along curved alignments.
Structural components that support bridge decks at their ends, utilizing inclined surfaces to distribute lateral forces and allow horizontal movement during superstructure expansion.
Steel structures designed to rotate about a pivot point at their base to accommodate differential settlement without bearing on concrete abutments.

Substructures supporting superstructures by allowing pivoting motions between the foundation and the bridge seat, accommodating superstructure movements without inducing additional shear or compression.
Structural supports that allow horizontal movement of a bridge deck by pivoting on curved surfaces to accommodate thermal expansion and contraction.
Steel structures supporting permanent gate cofferdams that pivot on a central pin to allow closure of a navigation lock chamber.
Structural members that support a bridge deck by allowing rotation to accommodate superstructure movement while maintaining load transfer through horizontal and vertical reactions.
A plot that represents the cyclic strength and ductility characteristics of a structural component by connecting points of maximum resistance at various deformation levels.

A curve that describes the fundamental relationship between the base shear force and roof displacement of a structural component under cyclic loading, representing its strength and deformation characteristics.
A curve representing the relationship between the strength and deformation of a structural component, derived from test data, used to assess its nonlinear behavior under cyclic loading.

A graphical representation derived from nonlinear static analysis that plots the relationship between lateral displacement and strength for a structural component or system, typically showing the yield point, peak strength, and post-peak behavior.
It represents the relationship between the vertical load and horizontal deformation of a structural component at various stages of loading, from initial yield to ultimate capacity.
A curve representing the peak and residual deformations of a structural component at specific force levels, used to quantify its force-deformation behavior under cyclic loading.
A graphical representation that plots the moment-rotation relationship of a structural component, showing its elastic and post-yield behaviors for structural analysis.

A plot representing the relationship between the effective yield strength and effective yield displacement of a structural component, derived from strain hardening curves and used to define its force-deformation characteristics.
Structural components that transfer lateral forces from concrete shear walls to the foundation by providing anchorage and continuity between these elements.
Components that transfer lateral forces from structural walls to the underlying foundation, maintaining structural integrity and stability.
Elements that transfer shear and overturning moments between structural walls and their supporting foundations.
Structural connections that transfer vertical and horizontal loads from reinforced concrete shear walls to the foundation, ensuring stability and preventing differential movement.
Connections between structural walls and their supporting foundations that transfer vertical and horizontal loads and maintain structural integrity.
Mechanical and structural connections that transfer loads from reinforced concrete shear walls to their underlying foundation elements.
Structural connections that transfer vertical loads and seismic forces between a wall and its supporting foundation while accommodating differential settlement.
Connections that transfer vertical and lateral loads from concrete or masonry walls to the foundation system.
A structural system designed to resist lateral forces by transferring them into vertical load paths without inducing significant in-plane bending moments in the braced wall segments.
Structural elements designed to resist lateral loads and maintain stability by preventing lateral displacement of columns or walls.
Structural components designed to resist out-of-plane forces and prevent excessive lateral movement in columns and other elements.
A structural component that resists horizontal forces applied to a column by providing rigidity and stability to maintain its alignment and prevent overturning.
A system used to resist horizontal forces and maintain stability in structural components by providing restraint across their width.
Structural elements that resist in-plane forces applied to seismic-force-resisting systems by transferring horizontal loads into vertical load paths.
A structural system that resists horizontal seismic forces by providing stability and preventing overturning in cribs and pile-supported structures.
A structural system that restrains transverse movement of structural components like columns or walls to prevent buckling under compressive loads.
Displacements of piles under load that can indicate their structural performance and potential failure modes.
The lateral displacements that occur in the vertical members of a retaining wall structure due to applied loads or movements.
Displacements within a pile group induced by relative settlement or differential movement between adjacent piles due to foundation interactions or soil-structure interactions.
Displacements of piles under load that may indicate soil-pile interaction and potential failure modes such as bearing failure or settlement under increasing loads.
The lateral movement of a pile under load, indicating its flexibility and resistance to lateral forces.
The lateral movement of a pile under lateral load, influenced by soil properties, pile embedment, and loading conditions.
Displacements of piles under load, calculated using the subgrade modulus method, which accounts for soil resistance along their length and at their tips.
Deformations in the longitudinal direction of a pile due to axial loading or bending caused by lateral forces.
A dimensionless coefficient that relates the ultimate bearing capacity of a soil to its effective overburden pressure and angle of internal friction.
A dimensionless coefficient used to calculate the bearing capacity of a strip footing based on the effective overburden pressure and the effective friction angle of the soil.
A dimensionless coefficient used to determine the ultimate bearing capacity of a foundation based on the effective overburden pressure and the soil's angle of internal friction.
A dimensionless factor used to estimate the bearing capacity of soil at depth by relating the effective overburden pressure to the soil's cohesionless strength.
A dimensionless factor used to calculate the ultimate bearing capacity of a shallow foundation that accounts for the influence of the soil's effective overburden pressure and frictional strength.
A dimensionless quantity derived from soil shear strength parameters to calculate the bearing capacity of shallow foundations under vertical load.
A dimensionless coefficient representing the bearing capacity of soil due to the overburden pressure that depends on the soil's friction angle.
A dimensionless coefficient that relates to the bearing capacity of a soil under a shallow foundation and depends on the soil’s angle of internal friction.
A layer of material applied to the cripple walls to reinforce them and provide a surface for attaching the flooring or other finishes.
A protective layer of materials applied to the vertical studs of a building's cripple wall to reinforce and stabilize it against lateral forces.
A structural element that covers the vertical framing between the foundation and first floor to support the house and allow access for utilities.
A layer applied over cripple walls to enhance their stiffness, stability, and resistance to lateral loads by connecting the wall studs together.
Wood sheathing applied to cripple walls to provide lateral support and stability.
A structural component that braces the top plate of cripple walls to resist lateral forces and distribute loads to the foundation.
A structural component that connects the foundation to the first floor framing, designed to resist uplift and overturning forces by providing lateral support and stability.
A layer of structural material applied to the outer surface of cripple walls to provide additional strength and resistance to lateral forces.
A method where a structural component is subjected to controlled, repeated loads simulating earthquake motions to evaluate its behavior and performance under realistic seismic conditions.
A method that subjects a structural component to repeated, controlled seismic forces to assess its seismic performance under actual load demands.
A series of experiments conducted on a structural component subjected to controlled, repeated loading cycles to evaluate its seismic response under simulated ground motions.
A method that applies mechanical forces to a structural component, replicating the dynamic effects of earthquakes, to evaluate its deformation and failure behavior under repeated seismic loading.

A method to assess a structural component's behavior under repeated, large-amplitude loading cycles applied at its full physical size, simulating the dynamic forces it would experience during an earthquake.
A method that subjects structural components to repeated large-amplitude loading cycles under controlled conditions to evaluate their seismic performance and behavior.
A test conducted on large-scale structural components subjected to repeated loading cycles that simulate seismic motions to evaluate their performance under dynamic conditions.

A testing method that applies simulated earthquake motions to an undamaged structural component to evaluate its performance under cyclic loading and assess potential damage accumulation and residual strength.
Material removed from channels, harbors, or other water bodies by dredging operations.
Substances removed from channels, waterways, or bodies of water through dredging operations, which may include sediments, soil, or debris.
Material excavated from the bottom of a water body during navigation maintenance or deepening operations.
A material excavated from underwater locations for the purpose of channel deepening or maintenance, often requiring environmental management and disposal considerations.
Material removed from a waterbody by dredging operations that may contain contaminants and requires management and disposal consideration.
Material removed from bodies of water by dredging operations that may be used for construction, environmental remediation, or other purposes.
It is material that is moved from beneath water by excavation or other removal methods for disposal or placement in another location.

Material that has been removed from its natural location, typically by dredging, which may include sediment, debris, or other substances that have accumulated in water bodies and are being placed elsewhere for management or disposal purposes.
A structural system designed to resist seismic forces and determine the seismic design forces and loads for other components of the building.

It is a structure designed to resist seismic forces through specific components like walls, braced panels, and their connections, with properties such as height, stiffness, and strength tailored to meet code requirements.
A system chosen as the basis for simplifying seismic design calculations, for which the calculated forces are intended to be applied directly.
A structural system specifically designed to resist seismic forces and whose performance is used to evaluate the adequacy of other structural components in a building.
A structural system designed to resist seismic forces through specific components and configurations as outlined in building codes, serving as the basis for structural analysis and design.
The fundamental structural system designed to resist seismic forces and transfer them to the foundation, serving as the primary basis for structural analysis and design.
A structural system designed to resist seismic forces based on specified performance criteria and modeled to produce a seismic response spectrum for evaluating other systems' performance.
The structural system specified by the code to determine seismic forces for establishing lateral design forces in a building.
The straight-line distance from the source of material to the location of the borrow area or stockpile where it will be deposited.
The distance over which excavated material must be transported to its final disposal or placement site.
The distance over which earth or rock is transported from a borrow area to a placement site in constructing an embankment.
The distance between the point where a material is loaded onto a truck and the point where it is unloaded and placed at its final location on a construction site.
The distance over which material is moved from a borrow area to the fill area during excavation or dredging operations.
The distance over which material is transported from the excavation site to its final disposal location.
The length over which excavated material is transported from the excavation site to its final disposal or reuse location.
The length of the road along which a truck or other vehicle travels to transport materials from a loading point to a designated unloading location.
A factor applied to the calculated deflection of a structural component to account for inelastic behavior in design.
A coefficient applied to the computed story drift to account for inelastic behavior during seismic loading.

A factor applied to the design story drift to account for the nonlinear behavior of structural components and the potential for higher deformations under seismic loading than predicted by elastic analysis.
A multiplier applied to the computed elastic displacement of a structural component to account for the effects of inelastic deformation and ductility in determining its design seismic force.
A numerical factor applied to calculated elastic deflections to account for inelastic behavior and reduce the risk of structural collapse in seismic design.
A multiplier applied to the elastic story drift to account for the system's inelastic behavior and energy dissipation capacity in seismic design.
A multiplier applied to the fundamental elastic response spectrum displacement to account for the inelastic deformation capacity of a structure under seismic loading.
A factor applied to the calculated elastic deflection of a structure to account for inelastic behavior and overstrength in seismic design.
The width of the concrete section that participates in resisting longitudinal reinforcement stresses through bond and shear transfer.
The portion of a structural member's cross-sectional area considered to participate in resisting longitudinal tensile stresses by acting compositely with the concrete deck.
The width of the concrete section that contributes to the stiffness and strength of a composite structural member in flexure.
The width of a concrete slab that acts compositely with a structural steel member to resist applied loads by sharing stresses and resisting bending moments together.
It is the portion of the concrete deck that acts compositely with the steel girder to resist applied loads by assuming uniform stress distribution over a specified width.

The width of a concrete slab that acts compositely with a steel girder, determined based on the slab's stiffness and proximity to the girder to calculate effective flexural stiffness and moment of inertia in composite design.
The portion of a structural member's cross-section that effectively contributes to resisting applied stresses under load.
The width of a concrete slab that acts compositely with a steel beam to resist longitudinal bending stresses in structural design.
The ratio of the maximum lateral displacement a structural component can sustain before losing its load-carrying capacity to its yield displacement.
A measure reflecting the ductility of a structural connection, quantified as the ratio of the inelastic rotation at connection failure to the yield rotation.
The parameter that quantifies the ability of a structural component to undergo inelastic deformations beyond its yield point without significant loss of load-carrying capacity.

A measure derived from the ratio of the cyclic ductility demand to the cyclic ductility capacity of a structural component to assess its ability to sustain deformation beyond its yield point during seismic loading.

A measure of a structural connection's ability to sustain deformation beyond its elastic limit without catastrophic failure, quantified as the ratio of its ultimate deformation to its yield deformation.
A measure of a structural component's ability to undergo inelastic deformation without fracturing, quantified as the ratio of energy dissipated to energy at yield.
A measure of a structural connection's ability to withstand large inelastic deformations under cyclic loading without brittle fracture or significant degradation of strength.
A measure of a structural component's ability to dissipate energy by deforming in a controlled manner under cyclic loading before fracturing occurs.
A device used to measure the resistivity of concrete at a specific location by applying a voltage and measuring the resulting current.
A device that measures the electrical resistivity of soil to estimate its moisture content by correlating with known calibration curves.
A device that measures the resistance of soil to penetration by a standard cone to estimate its bearing capacity and settlement characteristics.
A device used to measure the radiation level at a given location by detecting and quantifying the energy of penetrating radiation particles.
A device that measures the apparent resistivity of soil by injecting a current and measuring the resulting potential difference between two electrodes.
A device that measures the resistance of rock to penetration by a standard steel bar, providing an indirect assessment of rock hardness and potential drillability.
A device that measures the percentage of carbon, oxygen, or hydrogen in a material by bombarding it with alpha particles and detecting the energy of the particles that emerge.
A device used to measure and record the energy levels of seismic waves to classify earthquake magnitude on the Richter scale.

A laboratory procedure where clay suspensions are agitated to determine their fluidity and susceptibility to structural failure under shear stress, by assessing the highest concentration at which a sample remains liquid after settling and testing for structural integrity upon penetration with a jar or spoon.
A laboratory procedure that mixes water and flocculants to determine the optimal coagulant dosage and settle time for effective solid-liquid separation.
A procedure in which a sample of water is placed in a container and agitated to determine the optimal dosage of coagulant for effective particle removal.
A procedure that involves adding a coagulant to a water sample in a jar, mixing, and observing the resulting flocs to determine the optimal coagulant dose for coagulation treatment.
A procedure to visually observe and evaluate the flocculant properties of a coagulant by observing the settling behavior of particles in a jar.
A procedure that determines the optimal coagulant dosage by observing the formation of a "jar" or column of settled particles during laboratory testing.
A method to measure the coagulation effectiveness of test doses of chemicals by observing the sedimentation of flocculated particles in a jar.
A procedure that evaluates the effectiveness of coagulants by measuring the floc size and settling rate of suspended particles in a jar-shaped container.
A method where structural loads are transferred directly from the foundation to the soil without any intervening structural components.
A technique where seismic waves are transmitted directly through the soil mass to measure its shear wave velocity without the influence of a surface layer.
A technique where a motorized screw is inserted into a borehole and advanced by applying torque directly to the drill stem, with cutting tools or water jets to remove material as the screw turns.
A process where seismic waves are directly measured at the receiver site through geophones placed on the ground surface to assess subsurface conditions.
A technique where an instrument directly measures the time of arrival of seismic waves to determine the distance to the seismic source without needing reference points.
A method of monitoring for potential slope movement by directly observing and measuring changes in the horizontal and/or vertical distances between two points on a slope.
A method where seismic waves propagate directly from the source to the receiver, without being refracted or reflected by intervening layers.
A method where seismic wave velocity is determined by measuring the time taken for waves to travel directly between two points without refraction or reflection.
The process of draining fluids from a structure to prevent freezing by ensuring continuous water flow and removal of air and impurities from pipes.
A process in which excess slurry is removed from a surface by applying a vacuum to absorb the liquid component of the slurry.
A process in concrete construction where excess water is removed from a concrete mix by allowing it to drain out before placing the concrete into forms.
A gradual decrease in reservoir water level due to seepage through the dam and foundations.
A controlled release of water from a dam or reservoir to maintain a specified pool elevation or manage downstream flows.
A process in concrete construction where water is intentionally withdrawn from the concrete mix during placement to adjust its consistency and ensure proper compaction before final setting.
A process in which excess water is injected into a concrete structure to maintain a specified relative humidity within the curing environment.
A process in concrete construction where excess grout or mortar is removed from a preplaced-aggregate concrete structure by gravity drainage.
The process of moving a dredge pipe back and forth across a channel bed to remove sediment in a systematic pattern.
A process that gradually reduces the water depth in a dredged area to facilitate navigation, maintain channel depth, or remove dredged material for disposal or use.
A process that systematically maps the seabed by moving a transducer along a predefined path to generate high-resolution acoustic data.
A maneuver in which a vessel turns in the opposite direction of the intended course to avoid a hazard or obstacle.
A process where a steel element is systematically moved to cover and clean the bottom surface of a tank during repairs or inspections.
A process in which the end of a drill bit's cutting surface is pressed into the bottom of the hole to remove chips and debris.
A rapid surge of water that carries sediment through a channel, often initiated by dam removal or channel deepening.
A method of reducing the effective size of a detector element by moving it across a surface to collect data along a single line.
The maximum flood level that could reasonably be expected under the most severe meteorological conditions theoretically possible for a given watershed.
The flood that results from the most severe combination of hydrometeorological conditions reasonably possible for a given watershed.
The highest flood level a dam could theoretically experience based on the most extreme combinations of meteorological and hydrological conditions.
A flow magnitude derived from meteorological and hydrological conditions that represent the most severe natural event a dam could reasonably experience.
The highest flood level that could potentially occur as a result of the most severe natural meteorological and hydrological conditions, assuming the occurrence of all critical factors in combination.
The flood level calculated using the most severe combination of meteorological and hydrological conditions possible in a given watershed.
A hypothetical flood level resulting from the most severe combination of meteorological and hydrologic conditions that are deemed reasonably possible to occur, used to evaluate dam safety.
The highest water level that could reasonably occur based on the most severe natural meteorological and hydrological conditions and their most unfavorable combination.
A cylindrical, non-ferrous mechanical component with a smooth surface, primarily used as a bearing in the assembly of a steam engine's crankshaft.
A solid, pyramidal-shaped mass of masonry used to support the horizontal beam on a suspension bridge.
A tapered stone used to reinforce a masonry wall's corners or corners of openings.
A heavy, wedge-shaped stone used as a counterweight to balance the load on a derrick crane.
A flat, square stone used as the foundation and support for the lower section of a beam-and-block lift bridge.
A large, flat, irregularly shaped stone used to form the base of a derrick, providing stability and support.
A stone used to prevent the derrick from slipping down the hole during drilling operations.
A massive granite block used to support the upper part of a crane or derrick, typically placed atop a socket and secured by wedges to maintain stability and alignment during lifting operations.
A numerical assessment of a structure's overall condition based on its physical state and performance compared to established criteria.
A numerical value representing the current condition of a structural element, derived from a deterioration model based on age and previous inspections.
A numerical score indicating the current condition of a bridge deck relative to its initial condition, typically calculated based on visual field observations and analysis.
A numerical score assigned to a bridge component by an inspector to quantify its physical condition relative to specified criteria.
A numerical score assigned to a bridge component to quantify its current structural condition and performance.
A numerical measure assigned to a bridge component based on its observed condition, with 0 indicating deteriorated and 100 indicating new or undamaged conditions.
A qualitative assessment of the structural material's condition, based on visual inspection findings, which informs the need for repair or replacement.
A numerical assessment assigned to a bridge component to quantify its structural soundness and remaining service life.
A structural system where vertical bracing elements are designed to resist lateral forces in combination with the frame columns to achieve a dual system for seismic force resistance.

A structural system where the primary lateral force-resisting elements are braced walls connected to vertical elements such as columns and beams, designed to resist seismic forces by acting collectively as a rigid diaphragm.
A structural system where vertical elements are interconnected to resist lateral loads through relatively short, diagonal braces.
A structural system in which diagonal braces are placed between adjacent columns to resist lateral forces, with the diagonal members short enough to remain elastic under service loads.
A structural system where steel angles and plates are used as diagonal members to brace taller walls, transferring lateral loads to the foundation while allowing perpendicular movement.
A structural system where diagonal braces connect the top and bottom of a vertical column, forming a triangle to resist lateral forces.
A structural system where vertical elements resist lateral forces through direct connection to horizontal braces, without relying on shear resistance from diagonal struts.
A structural system with diagonal bracing elements that connect adjacent columns to resist lateral loads over a single bay.
The force applied to a bolted joint during assembly to ensure contact between mated surfaces and maintain tension under service loads.
The force applied to a bolt to compress its joint surfaces before external loading is applied, calculated to prevent slippage and maintain joint integrity under service conditions.
The tension applied to a bolt during installation, intended to resist external loads and ensure a secure connection.
The force applied to a fastener during initial assembly to ensure it remains tight under service loads.
The tension applied to a bolt or threaded fastener before it is installed, ensuring sufficient contact force between connected surfaces.
The force applied to a bolt during installation to compress the joint and resist loosening under service loads.
The applied force that tightens the bolt to the specified tension before any external loads are applied to the joint.
The axial tension intentionally introduced into a bolted connection during assembly to ensure it remains fully seated and functional under applied loads.
Specified values of seismic forces derived from structural analysis that govern the sizing and detailing of structural components to resist earthquake loading.
Prescribed magnitudes of seismic forces derived from spectral acceleration response values at specific periods, used to determine structural member demands.
Loadings, typically based on seismic coefficients, that represent maximum demands to which structural components must be capable of resisting during their design life.
Values representing the maximum loads a structural component must be capable of resisting to ensure safety under anticipated seismic loading.
The forces derived for structural components by multiplying their factored loads with the appropriate resistance factors or amplification coefficients.
The amplified loads calculated by multiplying nominal seismic loads by specified response modification, overstrength, and redundancy factors to ensure structural safety under seismic conditions.

Quantitative values of forces derived from analytical procedures that represent the anticipated seismic demands on structural components to ensure adequate safety and performance during earthquake loading.
The forces assigned to individual structural components based on the results of a structural analysis, calculated considering the seismic response spectrum and associated amplification factors.
A measure representing the maximum horizontal velocity of soil particles during ground motion, used to assess seismic site response and potential liquefaction.
The maximum velocity attained by a particle in a wave as it propagates through a medium.
A measure of ground motion intensity representing the maximum velocity attained by a particle in the soil due to an earthquake.
A measure of ground motion intensity derived from the maximum horizontal velocity experienced by a particle at the Earth's surface during an earthquake event.
The maximum horizontal velocity at which a soil particle moves during a seismic wave's passage.
The maximum velocity of a particle in the ground caused by seismic waves, often used to assess potential liquefaction hazards.
The maximum velocity of a particle in a wave during its passage through a material, used to assess potential damage in seismic ground motion analyses.
The maximum speed at which a particle in a seismic wave moves perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
A condition where excessive water infiltration causes the concrete's pore structure to become filled with water, thereby reducing its compressive strength and durability.
A condition where soil particles become completely surrounded by water, leading to a loss of shear strength and stability during liquefaction.
Damage to a soil specimen caused by repeated loading cycles that reduce its shear strength and stiffness due to progressive accumulation of plastic strains.
A condition in which soil particles become fully immersed in water, leading to a loss of structural integrity as their load-bearing capacity diminishes.

It is the progressive loss of structural capacity in a foundation due to the gradual degradation of soil strength and stiffness caused by repeated cyclic loading, leading to potential failure under subsequent seismic events.
A deterioration in a soil's engineering properties caused by the accumulation of excess pore water pressure during loading cycles, leading to reduced shear strength and increased compressibility.
A condition where subgrade soil reaches its maximum water content, leading to loss of bearing capacity and potential failure of pavements.
A phenomenon in soils where repeated cyclic loading causes progressive loss of strength and stiffness due to the gradual buildup of excess pore water pressure and decreased inter-particle contact.
The fraction of sediment entering a reservoir that remains impounded and does not pass through the dam.
The percentage of sediment that accumulates in a reservoir due to the interaction between flow characteristics and channel geometry, affecting the reshaping of the reservoir bed and storage capacity.
The percentage of sediment that a reservoir retains within its storage capacity over a specified time period.
The fraction of runoff captured and retained by a pond over a specified time period, calculated as the ratio of total ponded water volume to the total inflow volume during that period.
It is the ratio of the amount of sediment retained within a reservoir to the total sediment load entering the reservoir, measured over a specified period.
The fraction of a pollutant that remains in a sediment trap due to deposition or resuspension processes affecting its concentration over time.
The portion of sediment that settles out and remains within a sediment trap due to gravitational settling and exclusion by hydraulic conditions.
The ratio of the volume of sediment retained by a reservoir to the total volume of sediment entering the reservoir over a specified period.
A lateral force that approximates earthquake shaking by representing it as a fraction of the structural weight, adjusted for seismic intensity and building height.

A component of earthquake ground motion that acts horizontally on a structure due to the horizontal acceleration of its foundation, simulating the dynamic interaction between the foundation and the supporting soil.
A force applied horizontally to a structure to simulate the effects of seismic inertia acting on its center of mass.

A horizontal inertia force applied to building components in a direction perpendicular to the seismic loading, calculated to simulate the effects of lateral acceleration on nonstructural elements during an earthquake.
A horizontal force representing the seismic inertia of a structure's mass assumed to act at its center of mass, calculated as the product of the structure's mass and the design seismic acceleration.
A horizontal force applied to a structural model to simulate the seismic inertial effects acting on its mass.
A force applied horizontally to represent the inertial effects of seismic ground motion on a structure in analysis.
A force representing the horizontal inertial effects of ground motion applied to a structure as if acting laterally at each mass level to simulate dynamic behavior.
A horizontal line extending from the center of a bearing toward the center of the next bearing on the same line, used for aligning and referencing bridge components.
A standardized tool used to measure the depth of water in a well during a pumping test to monitor water levels.
A reference line established with a plumb bob that aligns with a datum to ensure the accuracy of subsequent measurements.
A device consisting of a weighted string used to measure the depth of water in a structure's damp-proof course.
A steel element that transmits axial tension from a post-tensioning tendon across a beam web to distribute the tensile force.
A device used to measure clearances between the bottom of a structure and a reference datum, consisting of a weight attached to a marked line.
A device used to determine water depth by measuring the length of a weighted line lowered into the water until it touches the bottom.
A wire used to guide and position temporary shoring tubes during their insertion into the foundation soil.
The factor used to modify the seismic response modification factor (R) based on the yield strength and ductility of structural components.
Stiffness factor that characterizes the soil's resistance to lateral movement under loading, derived from the elastic modulus.
A coefficient representing the ratio of the initial shear stiffness of a structural component to its elastic shear stiffness, used to adjust seismic force demands in analysis.
The ratio of the effective shear modulus to the shear modulus at zero shear strain, used to calculate the effective shear modulus of soil under large strain levels.
A factor representing the ratio of the shear stiffness of a structural diaphragm to that of a rigid diaphragm, used to adjust design forces.
A factor representing the fraction of the seismic shear force resisted by the structural wall, derived from the relative stiffness and distribution analysis within the structural system.
The ratio of actual peak ground motion to the peak ground motion predicted by a ground motion model for a given site.
A coefficient representing the ratio of the effective elastic foundation stiffness to the modulus of elasticity for the pile material in a pile-foundation interaction model.

A ground motion representing the maximum seismic demand that a structure might experience without incurring significant damage, used to evaluate its potential for collapse under extreme shaking, determined by multiplying the spectral response at the structure's fundamental period by a factor of 2.5.
An earthquake intensity defined as the maximum ground motion that a building can sustain while still maintaining its structural integrity and resisting collapse.
An earthquake event used to evaluate the probability of structural collapse, defined by a specific ground motion level derived from structural analysis and hazard curves.
A ground motion intensity that can cause structural failure under specific loading conditions, determined through nonlinear analysis and acceptance criteria.

An earthquake level representing the maximum ground motion intensity at which a structure may still sustain significant damage but not necessarily collapse, as defined by the collapse prevention performance level.

An earthquake ground motion level used to assess structural collapse risk, determined by analysis under extreme loading conditions and adjusted to account for the probability of exceedance within a specified time period.
An earthquake intensity defined as the maximum ground motion that a structure can withstand without structural collapse, determined through nonlinear response history analysis.
An earthquake with a defined ground motion intensity used to assess whether a building's design and structural elements can withstand seismic forces without risking collapse.
A numerical coefficient that scales the base shear demand for structural walls by accounting for their interaction with adjacent ground-floor columns and their connection to the foundation.
A coefficient applied to the seismic design forces for ground level walls to account for their proximity to the ground and the assumed rigidity of the soil supporting them.

A numerical value applied to seismic base shear calculations to account for the height-dependent reduction in lateral forces for walls in buildings with 4 or more stories where the height of the wall exceeds the height of the structural system.
A coefficient applied to the design seismic forces for ground level walls to account for their unique behavior and stiffness properties compared to other structural elements.
A coefficient that adjusts the expected lateral force demands on ground-level walls to account for the interactive effects of the superstructure and foundation on seismic soil-structure interaction.

A numerical value applied to seismic base shear calculations for ground level walls to account for their unique behavior and interaction with adjacent structural elements, which can enhance or reduce their seismic resistance compared to conventional walls.

A numerical factor applied to adjust the equivalent lateral force in design equations to account for the specific geometric and structural characteristics of ground level walls without openings, influencing their seismic resistance.
A coefficient applied to adjust the seismic design forces for ground level walls based on their proximity to and interaction with adjacent soil and other structural elements.
The ratio of the change in applied load to the corresponding change in deformation at the origin of a load-displacement curve, representing the tangential slope of the curve at zero load.
The modulus that characterizes the relationship between stress and strain in a material's elastic response under small deformations, representing the slope of the stress-strain curve at the origin.
A measure of a material's resistance to deformation under initial loading, determined by the slope of the stress-strain curve at very low stress levels.

A measure derived from the slope of the secant line connecting the origin and the point on the stress-strain curve corresponding to 50% of the maximum stress, characterizing the material's resistance to initial deformation.
The modulus of elasticity derived from the initial tangent to the stress-strain curve, representing the material's resistance to deformation under applied load.
The slope of the stress-strain curve at the origin, representing the material's resistance to deformation under load.
The modulus of elasticity representing the slope of the stress-strain curve at the origin, used to predict the deformation of structural components under applied loads.
A measure of the slope of the stress-strain curve at zero stress that quantifies the material's resistance to deformation under initial loading.
Alternative energy systems that provide electricity to a building or facility when the normal power source fails or is interrupted.
Alternative energy sources that are activated to provide electricity when the primary power supply fails.
Alternate energy sources that provide electrical power to critical systems in the event of a primary power outage.
Mechanisms that provide alternative energy sources to maintain critical systems functionality during primary power disruptions.
Mechanical, electrical, or electronic systems designed to provide uninterrupted power to critical equipment during primary power outages or failures.
Mechanisms designed to provide alternative electrical energy sources, such as generators or batteries, to maintain essential operations in the event of a main power outage.
Systems designed to provide uninterrupted electrical power to critical loads during grid outages or equipment failures.
Measures implemented to maintain operational capabilities of a facility or system by providing alternative electrical power sources in the event of a primary power outage.
Plants that extract water from the groundwater table and affect seepage in levees and dikes.
Trees and shrubs that draw water from the water table, modifying hydrological conditions at project sites.
